1-21.name: St. Cyprian, the Bishop, and St. Justina
1-21.summary: Cyprian was a pagan sorcerer and magician who had learned sorcery and magic from a young age and became famous for it, while Justina was a Christian virgin from Antioch who had vowed her virginity to the Lord. A young man who desired Justina asked Cyprian to use his magic to win her, but Justina's prayers and the sign of the Cross defeated every demonic attempt against her, and Cyprian's demons confessed their weakness before Christ. Cyprian therefore burned his books of magic, believed in the Lord Christ, was baptized, became a deacon, then a priest, and finally bishop of Carthage, with Justina as a deaconess and abbess of a convent. Both were arrested in the persecution of Diocletian, tortured severely, and, after refusing to deny Christ, were beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

1-22.name: Sts. Cotylas (Kobtlas) and Axoua, his Sister, and Tatas, his Friend
1-22.summary: Cotylas and his sister Axoua were the children of Shapur, King of Persia, who worshipped fire and the sun and persecuted believers in the name of the Lord Christ in his kingdom, and Cotylas's friend Tatas was a ruler over one of the countries under Shapur. Evil men accused Tatas before the king of being a Christian, so the king sent the governor to verify his faith and, if true, torture him, and Prince Cotylas also went to his friend. When the governor found Tatas to be a Christian, he ordered him thrown into the fire, but Tatas made the sign of the Cross over the fire and it was extinguished at once. Cotylas marvelled and asked how he had learned this magic, and Tatas replied that it was not magic but faith in the Lord Christ, and that with faith Cotylas could do even more, so Cotylas believed, drew near the fire, made the sign of the Cross over it, and the fire backed away a distance of fifteen cubits. The governor reported this to the king, who ordered Tatas beheaded, while Cotylas was tortured in various ways and cast into prison, and Axoua was sent to persuade him to abandon his belief. Instead Cotylas preached to her, turned her heart to faith in the Lord Christ, and sent her to a priest who baptized her secretly; she returned to her father saying she wished he had what her brother and she had, for there is no God but Jesus Christ, and the enraged king had her tortured until she yielded up her soul. Cotylas was then tied to the tails of horses and dragged over the mountains until he yielded up his spirit, his body was cut into pieces and cast out for the birds to consume, and after the soldiers departed, a saintly priest and a deacon went secretly at night and took his holy body, shining as snow, and hid it until the end of the days of persecution.

1-22.name: St. Julius of Aqfahs (El-Akfehasi), the Writer of the Biography of Martyrs, and his companions
1-22.summary: Julius was born in Aqfahs and, when he grew up, went to live in Alexandria, during the persecution incited by Emperor Diocletian and his comrades against Christians, especially the Copts of Egypt, for their devotion to faith in the Lord Christ and their disobedience to the emperor's orders to worship idols. Julius was very rich, and the Lord appointed him to care for the bodies of the holy martyrs, shroud them, and send them to their hometowns; he ministered to them himself and also used three hundred young men for this purpose, supplying them with funds and sending them to different parts of the country, where they wrote the biographies of the martyrs, shrouded them, and buried them, while the Lord distracted the governors so that no one objected to or captured him or forced him to worship idols. The martyrs he served blessed him, saying he must shed his blood in the name of the Lord Christ so that he would also be counted among the martyrs, and the Lord then appeared to him in a vision at night and commanded him to go to Arkadius, governor of Samanoud, and confess the Lord Christ before him. Julius went as commanded and was severely tortured, but the Lord strengthened him; when ordered to worship the idols, he prayed and the earth opened and swallowed up the seventy idols and the forty priests serving them, and the governor, seeing the destruction of his idols and priests, believed in the Lord Christ. The governor then went with Julius to the governor of Athribis, who tortured them much, but Julius prayed and the Lord sent an angel who cut off the heads of the idols and blackened their faces with ashes in the temple, and the governor of Athribis and a large number of people believed. Julius then went with the governors of Samanoud and Athribis to Iskandaros, governor of the city of Towa, who first refrained from torturing them but later ordered their heads cut off; Julius, his two sons Tadros and Yunias, his slaves, the governors of Samanoud and Athribis, and many people, numbered at 1,500, were martyred and received the crowns of martyrdom, and believers relocated the body of St. Julius, with the bodies of his two sons, to Alexandria.

1-23.name: Sts. Eunapius (Onanius) and Andrew, his Brother
1-23.summary: Eunapius and Andrew were two righteous brothers, sons of one of the nobles of the city of Lydda in Palestine, who in their youth agreed on the monastic life, went to a monastery in Syria and became monks, and shortly after went to the great St. Abba Macarius in the wilderness of Scetis, where they were his disciples for thirty years in love, humility, fasting, and continual prayer, and became well known for asceticism and knowledge. Eunapius was chosen as bishop and Andrew as priest, and they shepherded their flock with the best care, until the infidel Emperor Julian heard of them, had them brought before him, and tried to persuade them to deny faith in the Lord Christ. They refused, were tortured severely, could not be turned away, and were ordered beheaded, receiving, as the entry says, three crowns each: for monasticism, for priesthood and service, and for witnessing to the Lord Christ in martyrdom, in the year 79 of the martyrs (363 A.D.).

1-23.name: The Commemoration of the Martyr St. Thecla
1-23.summary: Thecla is presented as the first female martyr, the bride of Christ, a deaconess and disciple of the Apostle Paul, and an example of virginity and purity and a model for strife and enduring hardships. She was a native of Iconium, one of the cities of Asia Minor, of honorable pagan parents, very beautiful and well mannered, and engaged to one of the nobles of that city. When St. Paul came to Iconium on his first missionary journey, between 45 A.D. and 50 A.D., Thecla heard his preaching, marvelled at his teachings and followed him, believed in the Lord Christ, was baptized, vowed her virginity to the Lord, and broke off her engagement, turning from concern for physical beauty to care for spiritual adornment. Her mother, enraged when Thecla told her she had become a Christian and vowed her virginity, went to the governor of the city, who tried to convince Thecla to abandon Christianity and return to the worship of the gods and to her fiance; she utterly refused and did not heed his threats, was ordered burned to death, but a storm providentially extinguished the flames and she safely escaped death. She then left her city looking for St. Paul, who took her with him to Antioch and left her there to serve among the women; the governor there seized her and cast her to the wild beasts, which did not harm her, then threw her into a pit full of poisonous snakes, which also did not harm her, so he ordered her release. Paul encouraged and strengthened her and sent her back to her birthplace Iconium to preach the life-giving faith, but when her mother still insisted on pressuring her to return to paganism, she left Iconium and went back to Tyre in Syria to pursue her ministry, through which many believed. In the later part of her life she lived in seclusion, contemplation, and asceticism, God granted her the gift of healing and many were cured by her prayers, and finally she reposed in the Lord at ninety years old and was buried in Seleucia, the port of Antioch; the church calls her the martyr without shedding blood.

1-24.name: St. Quadratus, One of the Seventy Disciples
1-24.summary: Quadratus was born in Athens and was one of its great philosophers and learned nobles. When he believed in the Lord Christ, the Lord chose him to be one of His seventy apostles, and having received the grace of the Comforter on the day of Pentecost, he preached the life-giving Gospel in many countries, enlightened their people with the faith of the Lord Christ, and baptized them. Finally he returned to Athens, his birthplace, to preach Christianity there also, where he was seized and tortured severely, then cast into the fire, and thus received the crown of martyrdom.

1-24.name: St. Gregory, the Theologian
1-24.summary: Gregory of Nazianzus, the Theologian, departed on this day in the year 107 of the martyrs (391 A.D.); he was the son of Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, and was born in 328 A.D. in Arianzus, a village in Cappadocia not far from Nazianzus. As a young man his father sent him to schools in Caesarea of Cappadocia, Caesarea of Palestine, then Alexandria and finally Athens, where he learned logic, poetry, philosophy, rhetoric, and theological subjects, spending twelve years studying, during which he befriended St. Basil the Great, and both agreed on a life of devotion and monasticism. On returning home he assisted his aged father in pastoral care, was ordained a presbyter by his father in 361 A.D., and when Basil was consecrated archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Basil consecrated his friend Gregory as bishop for Sasima in 372 A.D., but Gregory could not go to his parish because it was disputed between Basil and Anthimus, bishop of Tyana, and the soldiers of the Arian Emperor Valens prevented him from entering it. He returned to Nazianzus to assist his father in his episcopal duties, and after his father's departure in 374 A.D. went to a monastery to live in seclusion for worship and contemplation for five years, then went to Constantinople in 379 A.D. because its Orthodox congregation urged him to come, since the Arians had troubled them with corrupt teachings, and there he returned many Arians to the Orthodox faith. The intention was to confirm him as patriarch of Constantinople, but when the Second Ecumenical Council convened in 381 A.D., those assembled studied the nomination and the Egyptian delegation objected because he had previously been consecrated bishop for another parish, so he left Constantinople after bidding the bishops and congregation farewell in a very moving letter. He then went back to Nazianzus to oppose the heresy of Apollinaris, later lived in seclusion in Arianzus, his birthplace, with some hermits, composed many articles against the Arians and other heresies, and composed the Five Theological Orations on the Divinity of the Logos, which earned him the title The Theologian; the Gregorian Liturgy is also attributed to him, and finally he reposed in the Lord.

1-24.name: St. Gregory, the Monk
1-24.summary: Gregory the Monk was the son of pious, Christian, and exceedingly rich parents from one of the cities of Upper Egypt, who cared greatly to teach him every virtue and educated him in the art of speaking, medicine, and also Church subjects; they later took him to Abba Isaac, bishop of their parish, who ordained him a deacon. He was inclined to the solitary life from his youth, used to pay many visits to Abba Pachomius of the Koinonia, later became a monk under Pachomius's guidance, and advanced greatly in the way of righteousness for thirteen years. When St. Macarius the Alexandrian came to visit the Cenobitic monasteries, Gregory asked Pachomius for permission to go back with Macarius to the mount of Kellia, the Cells; he dwelt with Macarius for two years, then, with Macarius's permission, dug out a small cave for himself in the mountain where he dwelt for seven years, visiting Macarius twice a year, on the feasts of the Nativity of the Lord and His Holy Resurrection, to consult him in his spiritual fight. When he had completed his good strife, the angel of the Lord informed him that after three days he would depart from the world, so Gregory called the elders of the desert, bade them farewell, and departed in peace on the third day.

1-25.name: Jonah, the Great Prophet
1-25.summary: Jonah was the prophet sent by the Lord to Nineveh to preach repentance to its people. He first fled from that command toward Tarshish, boarded a ship, and, when a great storm arose, the lot fell on him, so he was thrown into the sea and swallowed by a great fish, in whose belly he remained three days and three nights, prayed to the Lord, and was then vomited out onto dry land. He then went to Nineveh and preached that the city would be overthrown, and the king and people repented with fasting and sackcloth, so God forgave them; Jonah was angry at this mercy, sat outside the city under a plant that God prepared for shade, and, when a worm destroyed the plant, God taught him compassion for Nineveh and its many people. He is remembered as the great prophet whose three days in the fish prefigured burial and resurrection, and the entry commemorates his departure in peace.

1-25.name: St. Maurice, the Leader of the Theban Legion
1-25.summary: Maurice was the leader of the Theban Legion, a legion of Christian soldiers from Egypt. When the emperor Maximian ordered the legion to sacrifice to the idols and to persecute Christians, Maurice and his soldiers refused to deny Christ or to attack their fellow Christians, and, after the legion was twice decimated for its refusal, Maurice and his companions were beheaded at Agaunum and received the crown of martyrdom, with a church later built in their honor there.

Second Melody: Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion

1-26.name: St. Eustathius (Eustace), his Wife and his Two Sons
1-26.summary: St. Eustathius was at first a pagan and a minister of the Roman Empire during the reign of Emperor Trajan (98-117 A.D.). While hunting deer in the desert, as was his custom, he saw a figure of a cross reaching to heaven and heard the voice of the Lord Christ calling him to adopt the faith. He told his wife and two sons, went to the bishop of Rome, who taught them the faith, baptized them, and changed his name to Eustathius. Hardships like those of Job the righteous then befell him: he lost his slaves, maidservants, and all his possessions, left Rome because of poverty, and on the way lost his wife and two sons, but by God's divine providence they found one another again and rejoiced greatly at their reunion. When Emperor Hadrian reigned (117 A.D.) and heard they had become Christians, he summoned them, ordered them to offer incense to the idols, and they refused; hungry vicious beasts released on them did not harm them. Finally he placed them in boiling oil, so they delivered up their souls into the hand of the Lord and received the crown of martyrdom.

1-27.name: St. Eustathius, his Two Sons and his Wife
1-27.summary: St. Eustathius was at first a pagan and one of the ministers of the Roman Empire during the reign of Emperor Trajan (98-117 A.D.), gave alms and charity in abundance, and was very merciful to the poor. While hunting deer in the desert, he saw a figure of a cross reaching to heaven and heard the voice of the Lord Christ calling him to adopt the faith. He told his wife and two sons what had happened, went to the bishop of Rome, who taught them the faith, baptized them, and changed his name to Eustathius. Many hardships like those of Job the righteous came upon him: he lost his slaves, maidservants, and all his possessions, left Rome because of poverty, and on the way lost his wife and two sons, but by God's divine providence they found each other again and rejoiced greatly for their reunion. When Emperor Hadrian reigned (117 A.D.) and heard they had become Christians, he summoned them, ordered them to offer incense to the idols, and they refused; hungry vicious beasts released on them did not harm them. Finally he placed them in boiling oil, so they delivered up their souls into the hand of the Lord and received the crown of martyrdom.

1-28.name: Sts. Abadir (Apater) and Era-ee (Erini), his Sister
1-28.summary: Sts. Abadir and Era-ee, his sister, were the children of Wasilides' sister, who was a minister in the Roman Empire, and were born and raised in Antioch; Abadir was appointed Esfeh-selar, a high-ranking military position in Diocletian's army. When Diocletian renounced his faith in the Lord Christ and started to persecute the Christians, the Lord Christ appeared to Abadir in a vision at night and asked him to go with his sister Era-ee to Egypt to receive the crown of martyrdom, and his sister also saw that same vision that night. They left joyfully to fulfil what the Lord had ordered them, arrived at Alexandria and then at Ansena, where they confessed the Lord Christ before Arianus, who tortured them severely, but the Lord strengthened them in the midst of these severe pains. The governor wrote their decree and ordered them to be beheaded, so they received the crown of martyrdom; some believers took their bodies and shrouded them, and a deacon called Samuel took their bodies to his house, and when the era of persecution ended, a great church was built for them. In the present time there is a church after their names in Assiut and another one in Dashlout, district of Dyriut, Assiut governorate.

Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saints Apatir and His Sister Irini

1-29.name: The Commemoration of the Three Major Feasts of the Lord
1-29.summary: The church arranged a celebration on the 29th of each Coptic month to commemorate the three major feasts of the Lord: the Annunciation, Nativity, and Resurrection of Our Savior. The rites of the service are in the joyful tunes, with the readings as mentioned in the Katamaros. As an exception, during the months of Tubah and Amshir the church does not celebrate this commemoration, for they represent the law and the prophets; they also come before the month of Baramhat, when the Annunciation of the birth of the Lord Christ was fulfilled.
hymnIds: Watos Psali for 29th of Every Coptic Month

1-29.name: St. Arbsima (Repsima), Agatha her Mother and the 72 Virgins
1-29.summary: On this day also, the holy virgins Arbsima, Agatha her mother, and 72 virgins were martyred during the reign of Emperor Diocletian. The tyrant sought the most beautiful damsel to marry and sent some of his councilors to every country to search for her; when they arrived nearby Rome, they entered a convent for virgins and found Saint Arbsima, and none was like her in beauty, so they returned to the Emperor, described her to him, and he exceedingly rejoiced and sent to the kings and governors to invite them to the wedding celebration. When Arbsima and the virgins knew that, they wept, left the convent fleeing, entreating the Lord Christ to help them and keep their virginity, and fled to the country of Armenia, to the province of Tridates the king, where they dwelt in a winery in a desert garden, one of them making glass, selling it, and buying food for all of them with the money. Diocletian asked for Arbsima, searched diligently for her, learned she was in Armenia, and sent to Tridates the governor to look her up and return her to him; but when Tridates found her and saw her beauty, he wanted to have her for himself, and she did not let him. He brought her mother to persuade her, but instead she besought her to endure patiently, comforted her, and told her she must not forsake her true Bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ. When Tridates knew what her mother had done, he commanded her teeth to be broken and her to be slain; as for Arbsima, he ordered her to be tortured and then beheaded, and the soldiers tied her, tore out her tongue, plucked out her eyes, and cut her into pieces. Then Tridates ordered the rest of the virgins to be slain, and the soldiers killed all of them after torturing them severely, so they received the crowns of martyrdom.

1-29.name: St. Febronia (the Coptic Nun)
1-29.summary: On this day also, in the year 446 of the martyrs (750 A.D.), St. Febronia was martyred, during the papacy of Pope Khaeil I, the 46th Pope of Alexandria, and during the reign of Abdal al-Malik ibn-Marawan, who persecuted the Christians. Abu el-Abbas fought against him, so he fled with his army to Upper Egypt, and on his way ordered the destruction of churches and monasteries and the killing, plundering, and stealing of their valuables. Nearby Akhmeem there was a convent in which 30 nuns dwelt; after the soldiers plundered the convent, they found among the nuns one who was very beautiful, called Febronia, and wanted to take her and offer her as a present to the Sultan. When she heard that, she came forward to their leader, asked him for a respite, went to her cell, and prayed to God crying, asking Him to save her. She soon devised a way out: she entreated them to leave her for her worship in return for a favor she would do for them, namely a secret she had learned from her forefathers, an oil such that, if anyone anointed any part of the body with it, the sword would not harm him. To convince them, she anointed her neck with the oil and asked the leader of the soldiers to let the strongest of them strike her neck with all his might with his sharp sword; once he did that, the head of this chaste virgin was cut from her body and she received the crown of martyrdom. Great fear fell upon all the soldiers, and in haste they left the convent leaving behind all they had plundered, while her sisters the nuns took her pure body, shrouded her, and buried her with great veneration.

1-30.name: The Commemoration of the Miracle that God Performed for St. Athanasius the Apostolic
1-30.summary: On this day the church celebrates the great miracle the Lord Christ performed for the honorable Saint Abba Athanasius, the 20th Pope of Alexandria. When Emperor Constantius, son of the righteous Emperor Constantine, adopted the heretical teachings of Arius, he sent a man called Gawargios to Alexandria, along with 500 horsemen and letters appointing Gawargios patriarch of Alexandria instead of Abba Athanasius the Apostolic. When this man arrived in the city, he preached the erroneous teachings of Arius, but only a few people accepted his teachings, so he killed a large number of the people of Alexandria, while St. Athanasius hid himself for three years. Afterward Pope Athanasius went to Constantinople and asked Emperor Constantius either to restore him to his See or to slay him so he would receive the crown of martyrdom, and that was in the year 361 A.D. The Emperor instead ordered his men to place the saint in a small boat and leave him in the sea without food, water, or a guide, thinking he would die of hunger or drowning. By God's divine providence and watchfulness, the boat sailed smoothly and in peace, as if carried on the wings of angels, and he arrived at Alexandria three days later; when the believers heard their shepherd had arrived, they rejoiced, went out to receive him with candles and songs of praise, brought him into the church, expelled Gawargios and his followers, and St. Athanasius dedicated that day as a great feast to the Lord. No death or departure of St. Athanasius is described in this entry.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Athanasius the Apostolic
Melody for St. Athanasius the Apostolic (Thoout 30, Pashons 7)
Second Melody for St. Athanasius the Apostolic (Thoout 30, Pashons 7)

2-1.name: St. Anastasia
2-1.summary: St. Anastasia was martyred in 250 A.D. She was from Rome, of a wealthy family, and a disciple of the priest Chrysogonus. She comforted confessors and distributed her wealth to the needy. During the persecution of Emperor Decius she was arrested, tortured by being hung by her hair, beaten, cut, and finally beheaded by the sword, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

2-2.name: St. Severus, Patriarch of Antioch
2-2.summary: Severus was Patriarch of Antioch, born in Sozopolis in Pisidia, Asia Minor, in the middle of the 5th century, to wealthy parents. He was sent to Beirut to study law, was baptized, and became a monk in the monastery of St. Romanus. He was chosen Patriarch of Antioch in 512 A.D., defended the Orthodox faith against the Chalcedonians, was exiled by Emperor Justin, and departed in exile in Egypt in 538 A.D., in the time of Pope Timothy III.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Severus, Patriarch of Antioch
Melody for St. Severus Patriarch of Antioch

2-3.name: St. Siemon II, 51st Pope of the See of St. Mark
2-3.summary: Abba Siemon II departed in the year 547 of the martyrs (831 A.D.). He was born in Alexandria to Orthodox Christian parents who were among the nobles of the city, was raised on Orthodox principles and taught the church subjects, and chose the monastic life in the desert of Scetis, becoming a monk in the cell of his predecessor Abba Jacob, the 50th Patriarch, whose disciple he was for many years, exhausting his body by strenuous ascetic life and many worships. When Abba Marcus II became Patriarch, he requested Siemon from Abba Jacob because of his good reputation, sound judgment, and knowledge, and Siemon stayed with Marcus until Marcus's departure; when Abba Jacob then became patriarch, he kept Siemon with him and benefited from him often. After Jacob's departure, the bishops, priests, and elders unanimously chose Siemon as patriarch for his righteousness and true Faith, consecrating him on the 21st day of Amshir, year 546 of the martyrs (830 A.D.); he pursued an angelic life well-pleasing to the Lord, and, as God wished to repose him from the toils of this world, he remained on the throne only seven and a half months and departed in peace.

2-3.name: Sts. Ursus and Victor of the Theban Legion
2-3.summary: Ursus and Victor of the Theban Legion were martyred in the year 19 of the martyrs (303 A.D.). Coptic Reader presents them as soldiers of the Theban Legion who were martyred for the Christian faith under the persecution of that period, giving no further details about their lives or manner of death in the entry as checked.

2-3.name: Empress Theodora
2-3.summary: Empress Theodora departed in 547 A.D. She was the wife of Emperor Justinian. Her father was Acacius, a keeper of bears in Constantinople. She was a supporter of the Orthodox faith, and after her departure she was buried with honor.

2-3.name: St. John El-Ashruby (El-Gawhary)
2-3.summary: John was a soldier, born in Ashruba in the district of El-Bahnasa, to rich and pious parents named Theodor and Sophia, who were childless until an angel promised them a child described as a jewel, hence his name El-Gawhary. He joined the army and became a centurion. In the time of Diocletian's persecution he confessed Christ before the governor, was tortured, and was beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

2-4.name: St. Bacchus
2-4.summary: Bacchus was a friend of Sergius and an officer in the army of Emperor Maximianus. When they confessed Christ, they were stripped of their ranks and sent to Antiochus, king of Syria, who imprisoned Sergius and ordered Bacchus to be slain. Bacchus was beheaded, his body was weighted with stones and cast into the River Euphrates, the waves carried it to shore near holy ascetics, an angel told two of them to carry it, an eagle and a lion protected it, and it was carried with hymns to a cave and buried there.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saints Sergius and Bacchus
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saints Sergius and Bacchus
Doxology for St. Sergius and St. Bacchus

2-5.name: St. Paul, Patriarch of Constantinople
2-5.summary: St. Paul received the crown of martyrdom in the year 68 of the martyrs (351 A.D.). He was born in Thessalonica in the latter part of the third century, became from a young age a disciple of Abba Alexandros, Patriarch of Constantinople, and succeeded him on the patriarchal throne upon Alexandros's departure in 336 A.D. He fought tirelessly against the Arians, who denied the divinity of the Lord Christ, until he purged their influence from the region. When Emperor Constantius, son of Constantine the Great and an adherent of Arianism, ascended the throne of Constantinople, he demanded that Paul cease resisting the Arians; Paul steadfastly refused, was exiled multiple times from his See, and was ultimately banished to Armenia, where Constantius secretly instructed one of Arius's followers to kill him, and the assassin entered Paul's dwelling under cover of night and strangled him.

2-5.name: Anba Peter, Bishop of El-Bahnasa
2-5.summary: Anba Peter departed after becoming a monk in the monastery of Anba Shenouda the archimandrite, on Mount Adribah, west of Souhag. He devoted himself to studying and searching the Holy Scriptures and church books and became a brilliant scholar, especially in church rituals and hymnology. He was consecrated bishop of El-Bahnasa for the period 1186 to 1220 A.D., when El-Bahnasa was a great city and capital of a province since Pharaonic and Roman times, and a large parish including many churches, monasteries, and convents in the western desert nearby. He had many publications in church rituals, above all the readings and hymns of the Holy Pascha: building on the work of Pope Gabriel II, the 70th Pope, who with monks from St. Macarius monastery had organized the Pascha readings into five Morning Hours and five Evening Hours, Peter recognized that the Passion Week lectionary was not well-arranged, so he rearranged it, gathering appropriate prophecies and psalms from the Old Testament, including the deutero-canonical books, and Gospels from the New Testament for each hour, made the hourly readings more uniform in length, and published all these changes in the Katameros of the Holy Pascha, which the Church still uses today. He also arranged two sermons from the sayings of the fathers daily, one for morning and one for evening prayer; arranged for each of the four Gospels to be read in its entirety during Passion Week; arranged the reading of the whole book of Psalms, 151 psalms, on the evening of Good Friday after the Burial Procession and the Hymn of Golgotha; compiled and edited the commentaries of the prophecies and Gospels of Passion Week in a book still used to the present time; composed tunes for many prayers and readings, especially the Paschal psalms sung in the Adribic mourning tune; and introduced the Royal Tune to some Paschal psalms. His other publications were the rites of the Lakkan of the feast of the fathers the Apostles, and the rites of consecrating new Baptisteries, still used today. When the days of his service were completed, he departed in peace and went to his eternal home to rest.

2-6.name: The Righteous Hannah, the Mother of Samuel the Prophet
2-6.summary: Hannah was of the tribe of Levi and the wife of Elkanah, son of Jeroham, whose other wife was Peninnah. She was barren and reviled, went yearly to the tabernacle at Shiloh, received a double portion, and wept and would not eat; she prayed in the house of the Lord before Eli the priest at the doorpost, vowing that if she bore a male child she would give him to the Lord all the days of his life and no razor would come upon his head. Eli first thought her drunk, then, learning she was a woman of sorrowful spirit, told her to go in peace and that God would grant her petition; she believed, ate, and her face was no longer sad. She conceived Samuel, whose name is explained as God has heard, weaned him, took him to the house of the Lord and gave him to Eli, lending him to the Lord as long as he lived, and praised God in the profound prayer recorded in the second chapter of 1 Samuel. She lived pleasing to God, the Lord visited her and she bore three sons and two daughters, and, having completed her good endeavor, she departed in peace.

2-7.name: St. Paul of Tammoh
2-7.summary: Paul of Tammoh departed in 418 A.D. He was born in Tammoh, was inclined from youth to worship and seclusion, and went to Mount Ansena with his disciple Ezekiel, exhausting his body by austere asceticism, fasting, and many prayers beyond human endurance, until the Lord appeared to him saying, Enough struggle, my beloved Paul, and Paul answered, Let me exhaust my body as You exhausted Yourself for mankind, after which the Lord consoled and strengthened him and ascended. St. Bishoy went to Mount Ansena after the first raid of the Berbers on the wilderness of Scetis in 407 A.D., and Paul received him with joy. An angel told Paul that his body would be with Bishoy; this was fulfilled when Bishoy departed on the 8th of Abib, year 133 of the martyrs (417 A.D.), and was buried there, and three months later Paul departed and his body was placed beside Bishoy. During the papacy of Pope Yousab I (830-849 A.D.), when it was wished to relocate the body of Anba Bishoy to his monastery in the wilderness of Scetis among his children the monks, the body was placed on a boat and the boat would not move; the righteous old monk Armia explained that the boat would not move with the body of Anba Bishoy alone because of the covenant between the two saints, so the body of Anba Paul was also carried with him, and the boat then moved, and both bodies were placed in the monastery of Anba Bishoy in the wilderness of Scetis.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Pishoy and St. Paul of Tammah

2-8.name: St. Matra the Elder
2-8.summary: St. Matra the elder was martyred in Alexandria. He was a pious Christian from the city of Alexandria. When the infidel emperor Decius reigned, he ordered the persecution of Christians in every place of the Empire; when his edict reached Alexandria, Matra was seized, brought before the governor, and confessed the Lord Christ. The governor commanded him to worship the idols and promised him splendid promises, which he refused, and then threatened and intimidated him with severe punishment. Matra did not change his conviction but shouted that he worshipped and knelt only to the Lord Christ, the creator of heaven and earth, and asked how he could forsake Him and worship idols made of stones and wood that do not hear or see. The governor became enraged and ordered him beaten; he was severely beaten and then hung up by his arms, imprisoned for a few days in a repugnantly smelling dark prison, then taken out, beaten again and wounded. Finally, when the governor saw him steadfast in his faith in the Lord Christ, he ordered St. Matra to be beheaded outside the city, so he received the crown of martyrdom.

2-8.name: Sts. Abba Or, Tosia (Susanna) and their Children
2-8.summary: Coptic Reader lists the martyrdom of Sts. Abba Or, Tosia, and their children on this day, but the Synaxarion page as checked gives this as a one-line commemoration with no further narrative about their lives, places, or manner of death.

2-8.name: Abba Agathon, the Hermit
2-8.summary: Agathon became a disciple of Abba Poemen in the wilderness of Scetis during the fourth century. When his teacher departed, he followed the instructions of St. Arsenius. He left the wilderness after the first raid of the Berbers on Scetis in the year 410 A.D. and lived on Torah mount. He strove to fulfill the Divine commandments, was simple in his clothing, led a pious ascetic life, owned only an iron knife to split the fronds and braid baskets, was said to be full of sweetness, gentleness, and enthusiasm, and was able, by his wisdom and renouncing the world, to gather around him many monks; he loved the virtue of giving and serving sojourners. One time he found a sick man lying on the side of the road, carried him to a hostel, and cared for and provided for him for four months; after the man was healed, Agathon went to the desert saying to himself that he wished he could find a leprous man to give him his body and he gave Agathon his body. He used to say that he never went to sleep angry at someone, and had the famous saying that if a man of wrath were to raise the dead, he would not be accepted by God, and the Paradise of the Fathers records for him many useful sayings. When his departure drew near, he spent three days in deep contemplation and said to those around him that he was occupied at that hour by meeting Christ, then departed in peace, his face shining and smiling as he met his beloved friend for whom he had longed.

2-9.name: Pope Omanious (Eumenes), the 7th Patriarch of Alexandria
2-9.summary: Pope Omanious (Eumenes) was the seventh Patriarch of Alexandria. He departed on this day in the year 129 A.D., after serving on the patriarchal chair for ten years, having been appointed after his predecessor's departure. During his patriarchate he ordained priests and deacons and cared for and established his flock in the faith. He departed in peace, not by martyrdom.

2-9.name: St. Simon (Simeon), the Bishop
2-9.summary: Coptic Reader presents a brief commemoration of St. Simon (Simeon), a bishop, giving his episcopal service and his peaceful departure, and no martyrdom or extended life story in the entry as checked.

2-10.name: St. Sergius, the Friend of St. Bacchus
2-10.summary: St. Sergius was the close friend and companion of St. Bacchus. He was a Christian who refused to sacrifice to idols under persecution, steadfastly confessing Christ despite torture. He was martyred by beheading with the sword, and his martyrdom is presented in connection with Bacchus, his fellow martyr and friend.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saints Sergius and Bacchus
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saints Sergius and Bacchus
Doxology for St. Sergius and St. Bacchus

2-11.name: St. James, the Patriarch of Antioch
2-11.summary: St. James was Patriarch of Antioch, a virtuous, ascetic patriarch who shepherded his flock, taught the Orthodox faith, and opposed heresy. He departed in peace after a life of pastoral care and teaching, not by martyrdom.

2-11.name: St. Pelagia, the Penitent
2-11.summary: St. Pelagia was a woman of Antioch who had lived a sinful, worldly life as a famous actress and dancer, adorned richly and accompanied by servants. Hearing the preaching of Bishop Nonnus, she repented, was baptized, gave away her wealth to the poor, and withdrew to Jerusalem, where she lived in strict asceticism disguised as a male monk named Pelagius. She departed in peace after her repentance and monastic life, and was only then recognized as a woman.

2-12.name: Archangel Michael (Monthly Commemoration)
2-12.summary: This is the monthly commemoration of the Archangel Michael, the great archangel and commander of the heavenly hosts. The page presents Michael as the intercessor and protector of God's people, the one who stands before God, defeats Satan, and carries out God's commands. It is a commemoration and feast entry, not the life or death of a human saint.
hymnIds: Doxology for Archangels Michael and Gabriel
Fraction to the Father for Archangel Michael
Archangel Michael (12th of Every Coptic Month)

2-12.name: St. Matthew, the Evangelist
2-12.summary: St. Matthew was one of the Twelve Apostles and the Evangelist who wrote the Gospel of Matthew. He was a tax collector called by Christ, who left all and followed Him, preached the Gospel, and wrote his Gospel for the Hebrews. He preached in Ethiopia and other lands, endured persecution, and was martyred there, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

2-12.name: St. Demetrius I, the 12th Patriarch of Alexandria, the Vinedresser
2-12.summary: St. Demetrius I was the twelfth Patriarch of Alexandria, known as the Vinedresser because he worked as a vinedresser before his election. He was chosen as patriarch in a miraculous way, a man carrying grapes being the sign, and he served the Church for many years, ordaining clergy and teaching the faith. He departed in peace in the year 230 A.D., after a long patriarchate, not by martyrdom.

2-13.name: St. Zacharias, the Monk, the Son of Cyrion
2-13.summary: St. Zacharias was a monk of Scetis and the son of Cyrion. He entered monastic life with his father in Scetis, lived in great asceticism, humility, and obedience, and was known for his purity and spiritual wisdom despite his youth. He departed in peace as a young monk, remembered as a model of monastic virtue.

2-14.name: St. Philip, One of the Seven Deacons
2-14.summary: St. Philip was born in Caesarea, Palestine. The Lord Jesus chose him as one of the Seventy Disciples, sent to preach and heal the sick, and the Apostles then chose him as one of the Seven Deacons appointed to serve. He preached in the cities of Samaria and baptized its people, including Simon the magician, who perished when he tried to buy the gift of the Holy Spirit with money. Directed by an angel to the road from Jerusalem to Gaza, he met the Ethiopian eunuch, minister of Candace, reading Isaiah, explained the scripture, preached Christ to him, and baptized him; the Spirit then caught Philip away, and he was found at Azotus, preaching through all the cities to Caesarea. He later traveled the countries of Asia preaching the Gospel, supported by many miracles, was married with four daughters who prophesied and preached with him, brought many Jews, Samaritans, and others to faith, and, when he had finished his good endeavor, departed in peace.

2-15.name: St. Panteleimon, the Physician
2-15.summary: St. Panteleimon the physician was martyred on this day in the year 21 of the martyrs (305 A.D.). He was born in the city of Nicomedia; his father worshipped idols, but his mother was a Christian. Educated as a physician, he excelled, and Emperor Maximian made him his private physician, appreciating his success, intelligence, and gentle demeanor. He met the priest Hermolaus, who taught him the Christian faith and baptized him; he reached a high level of virtuous life, and God worked great wonders by his hands, including healing a blind man immediately by making the sign of the Cross over his eyes in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. When the emperor learned of this, the blind man testified that Panteleimon healed him by the sign of the Cross; the emperor then questioned Panteleimon, who confessed he was a Christian, refused to renounce Christ despite riches, honors, threats, beating, flogging, and being cast into the sea and fire, Christ appearing to strengthen and comfort him, and was finally beheaded by order of the emperor, after fervent prayer, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

2-16.name: St. Agathon, 39th Pope of Alexandria
2-16.summary: Pope Agathon, the 39th Pope of Alexandria, departed on this day in the year 397 of the martyrs (681 A.D.). He was from a noble family in Marriot, and when he grew up he became a disciple of Pope Benjamin, the 38th Pope. Anba Benjamin ordained him a priest for one of the churches of Alexandria; when Benjamin hid for a time from his Chalcedonian persecutors, he left Agathon to preach to believers and establish them in the Orthodox faith, and Agathon went about disguised wearing a carpenter's apparel and carrying carpenter's tools, performing pastoral duties and celebrating the divine mysteries in secret, until Benjamin returned to the papal See and appointed Fr. Agathon as his private secretary. After Benjamin's departure, Agathon was chosen to the patriarchal rank and consecrated on the 14th of Tobe, year 387 of the martyrs (662 A.D.), facing great tribulations for keeping the Orthodox faith, notably from Theodorus, a Chalcedonian who went to El-Khalifa in Damascus, gave much money, obtained a decree appointing him Governor of Alexandria, El-Behira, and Marriot, then afflicted Anba Agathon, levied high taxes, severely persecuted him, and ordered that anyone finding the Patriarch should slay him, so Agathon detained himself in his cell until God destroyed that evil governor. During his days the building of St. Macarius' church in his monastery in the wilderness of Scetis was completed. One night the angel of the Lord told him of a holy monk from St. Macarius' monastery named John, ordered him to bring John to assist in preaching and teaching, and said John would be patriarch after him; Agathon brought him and entrusted him with church administration and teaching, and when Agathon completed his good endeavor he departed in peace.

2-16.name: Sts. Carpus, Apollo and Peter
2-16.summary: Coptic Reader lists the commemoration of the saints Carpus, Apollo, and Peter on this day, but the Synaxarion page as checked gives only a single sentence: they were disciples of the Holy Father Anba Isaiah of Scetis, with no further life, place, dates, or manner of death given.

2-17.name: St. Dioscorus II, 31st Pope of Alexandria
2-17.summary: Pope Dioscorus II, the 31st Pope of Alexandria, departed in the year 235 of the martyrs (518 A.D.). Born in Alexandria, he was taught and reared in Christian conduct, was gentle in disposition and righteous in deeds. After his predecessor Pope Youannes II, the 30th Patriarch, departed, the fathers of the church convened and chose him Patriarch on the 3rd of Baounah, year 232 of the martyrs (516 A.D.). On his enthronement to the See of St. Mark he wrote a catholic epistle to Anba Severus, Patriarch of Antioch, expressing the principles of Orthodox doctrine; Severus replied with a congratulatory message, which Dioscorus received with joy and ordered read to all the people. During his days a dissension in Alexandria angered Emperor Anastasius; the people, terrified of punitive measures, pleaded with the Pope to intercede, and he succeeded, with the Emperor declaring pardon for them. He sat on the throne of St. Mark for three years, preaching and teaching continually and urging priests in every city to shepherd and guard their flocks, and departed leaving his flock grieving for a spiritual shepherd like him.

2-18.name: St. Theophilus, 23rd Pope of Alexandria
2-18.summary: Pope Theophilus, the 23rd Pope of Alexandria, departed in the year 128 of the martyrs (412 A.D.). He was born in the city of Manf (Memphis) to rich Christian parents who died when he was young; an Ethiopian woman raised him and his sister, who later became the mother of St. Cyril, and when they grew up she brought them to St. Athanasius, Patriarch of Alexandria. Athanasius took Theophilus as his disciple, kept him close, and made him his secretary; Theophilus was later ordained a priest and, after Athanasius's departure, was chosen Patriarch in the year 101 of the martyrs (385 A.D.). He was knowledgeable, wise, learned in the scriptures, God-fearing, and a great preacher; his writings include homilies and a commentary on the book of Proverbs. He built churches, including churches of the Virgin and of St. John the Baptist, and a church for St. Raphael, with Theodosius the King giving him the Serapion temple, built for the idol Serapis, whose idols he destroyed, turning it into churches. After the departure of the emperor, his enemies accused him of burning books and causing dissension, and he was summoned to Constantinople to be judged, but the entry says he was cleared, returning to his flock after 27 years on the throne of St. Mark, with his final words being thanks to God and to the Virgin.

2-19.name: St. Theophilus and His Wife
2-19.summary: St. Theophilus and his wife, in the city of El-Fayyum, were martyred during the days of Emperor Diocletian. After being beaten, imprisoned, and tortured, the governor ordered them thrown into a deep pit and stoned to death; their bodies were buried in the pit under the stones. Coptic Reader gives no further life details for them in this short entry.

2-19.name: The Assembly of a Council in Antioch
2-19.summary: In the year 262 A.D., a holy council assembled in Antioch concerning Paul of Samosata, Patriarch of Antioch, who was a native of Samosata. The entry says Satan sowed in his heart the belief that the Lord Christ was an ordinary man and not the Son of God, and that he fell into blasphemy. Abba Dionysius, the 14th Pope of Alexandria, was invited to attend, but because of his old age and poor health he could not attend, and instead wrote a letter to the council; the bishops and clergy of Antioch also sent letters to the Patriarch of Alexandria. The council condemned Paul of Samosata and excommunicated him, and the entry says the Lord preserved the Church from his heresy.

2-20.name: The Great St. John Colobos (the Short)
2-20.summary: St. John Colobos, called the Short because of his short stature, was born in the year 339 A.D. in Thebes (Luxor) to righteous parents. At age 18 he went to Scete and became a disciple of Anba Pemwah, who tested him by making him water a dry palm branch for a year; the branch grew and bore fruit, and Pemwah saw an angel crowning him, saying he would be a chosen vessel. He was tonsured a monk and lived in great asceticism, fasting, prayer, and humility. When the Berbers attacked Scete he fled to a mountain, then returned; later he went to the mountain of Antony, and then to the wilderness of Qolzem. He had many disciples, including Anba Arsenius and Anba Daniel, and was known for his love, meekness, and miracles, including healing the sick and casting out demons. He departed in peace in the year 434 A.D., after a life of about 95 years, and his body was later returned to Scete.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. John the Short

2-21.summary: Coptic Reader lists the commemoration of the Holy Theotokos, the Virgin St. Mary, on this day, but the Synaxarion page as checked gives no further narrative beyond stating that the Church commemorates her and asks her intercession.

2-21.name: Joel the Prophet
2-21.summary: Joel the Prophet, son of Pethuel, of the tribe of Reuben, whose Hebrew name means Jehovah is God, was one of the twelve Minor Prophets. He prophesied in the days of Asa, son of Abia, son of Jeroboam, King of Judah, before Isaiah, while Amos prophesied in Israel. He incited the people to true repentance, prophesied the outpouring of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, the preaching of the Gospel from Jerusalem, and the final judgment and the second coming. He departed in peace in good old age and was buried in his field in Jerusalem.

2-21.name: The Relocation of the Body of Lazarus, the Beloved of the Lord
2-21.summary: After the Lord raised Lazarus from the dead, Lazarus fled from the Jews who sought to kill him, and went to the island of Cyprus, where he was made bishop of Kition by the apostles Paul and Barnabas. He lived there for 30 years after his resurrection, then departed in peace. His body was later relocated to Constantinople in the reign of Emperor Leo the Wise, and the entry says his relics were placed in a church built in his name in Constantinople.

2-21.name: Anba Roweis (St. Freig, Ava Tegi)
2-21.summary: Anba Roweis, also called St. Freig or Ava Tegi, departed in the year 1121 of the martyrs (1405 A.D.). He was a contemporary of Pope Mettaos I, and was from a small village in El-Gharbiah. He lived a life of great asceticism, poverty, and simplicity, wearing a simple garment and eating little, and was known for his miracles and for his love for the poor. He lived in a cell near the church of St. Mercurius in Old Cairo, and many came to him for prayer and blessing. He was a spiritual father to many, including bishops and priests, and he departed in peace, with his body buried in the church of St. Mercurius.

2-22.name: St. Luke the Evangelist
2-22.summary: St. Luke the Evangelist was martyred on this day in the year 67-68 A.D., during the reign of the tyrant Emperor Nero. Born in Antioch to pagan parents, he was raised, brought up, and educated as a physician, and was an eloquent speaker, writer, and painter who lived a celibate life; the Lord chose him as one of the 70 disciples. He accompanied the apostle Paul on his second missionary journey from Troas to Philippi and on his third journey from Philippi to Jerusalem, and accompanied Paul in Rome during his imprisonment; Paul loved him much and called him Luke the beloved physician who is working with me. He wrote his Gospel between the years 60-63 A.D., in the Greek language, for the Gentiles, portraying the Lord Christ as a Savior for all humanity, demonstrating Christ as human in His full humanity, resembling us in everything except sin alone, and depicting Him as the lover of sinners, healer of the sick, comfort of the fainthearted, and shepherd of the lost sheep; the symbol of his Gospel is the Ox, because he wrote about sacrifices and the atonement sacrifice of the Lord Christ. He also wrote the Acts of the Apostles as a continuation of his Gospel between the years 63-64 A.D., during his stay with Paul in his first imprisonment in Rome, dedicating it to the same person as the Gospel, the most excellent Theophilus. He was martyred by the orders of Nero at age 84, receiving the crown of martyrdom; his pure body was placed in a hair sack and cast into the sea, but by God's providence the waves threw the holy body onto an island, where a believer found it, shrouded it with costly shrouds, and buried it with great honor. His body was relocated to Constantinople in the reign of Emperor Constantius, year 357 A.D., along with the relics of St. Andrew, and later relocated again to Italy in the year 1177 A.D.

2-23.name: St. Dionysius, Bishop of Corinth
2-23.summary: St. Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in Greece, was martyred during the days of Diocletian and Maximianus (284-312 A.D.). He endured many severe tortures for the sake of his faith in the Lord Christ and for refusing to offer incense to the idols; when his persecutors saw his perseverance and were weary of torturing him, they cut off his holy head with the sword, and thus he received the crown of eternal glory.

2-23.name: St. Yousab, 52nd Pope of Alexandria
2-23.summary: Anba Yousab I, the 52nd Pope of Alexandria, departed in the year 566 of the martyrs (849 A.D.). He was the only child of his parents, who were from the city of Menuf, El-Menofia governorate; when his parents departed while he was still young, a certain rich family raised him. When he grew up he longed for the monastic life, so he went to the patriarch Pope Marcus II and revealed his desire; the Pope rejoiced and sent him to the monastery of St. Macarius in the wilderness of Shiheet, where he became a monk under the guidance of a holy old man. He lived a life of asceticism and piety; Pope Marcus II ordained him a priest, and he served with him in the patriarchate for a period of time, then returned to the wilderness. After the departure of Anba Simon II, the 51st Patriarch, the bishops and people asked God to make known whom He chose; the Lord guided them to this father, and they sent a delegation to the wilderness to bring him. On their way they prayed that, if God had chosen this father for this honor, the sign would be that they find his door open upon arrival; they found his door open, for he was bidding farewell to some visiting monks, and when he was about to close his door he saw them coming, received them with joy and welcomed them to his cell, where they seized him and told him Axios, meaning he is worthy. They took him to Alexandria, where they consecrated him patriarch on the 21st day of Hathor, year 548 of the martyrs (831 A.D.). He took great interest in building churches and teaching the people, but Satan became envious and brought much sorrow upon him: the bishops of Tinnis and Miser had brought many hardships upon their congregations, who appealed to the patriarch for help; Anba Yousab asked the two bishops often to be merciful to their flocks, but they would not accept his behest, and though he exerted great effort to reconcile them it was in vain, so the Pope convened a council and excommunicated them. The two bishops then went to the Governor in Cairo and brought false accusations against Anba Yousab; the Governor sent his brother with soldiers to bring the Patriarch to him, and when they came, the Governor's brother drew his sword to kill him, but the Lord thrust aside his hand and the sword struck a pillar and was broken; furiously, the Prince drew his dagger and drove it with all his might into the side of the father, but the dagger did not harm the Patriarch other than cutting his apparel. Realizing the Patriarch had divine grace and heavenly protection, the Prince brought him with respect to his brother and told him what had happened; the Governor also respected and feared him, asked him about the accusations, and the Patriarch proved their falsehood and informed him of the truth about the two complaining bishops. The Governor was convinced, honored the Patriarch, and wrote for him a decree that no one should disobey him in any ordination or removal of any bishops or in any other work concerning the church. The Lord wrought many miracles by his hands; he continually preached to the sinners and admonished the disobedient, establishing the people in the Orthodox faith. After having sat on the throne of St. Mark for 18 years, he departed in peace.

2-24.name: Abba Hilarion, the Monk
2-24.summary: The great Saint Anba Hilarion departed in the year 87 of the martyrs (371 A.D.). Born at Tabatha, south of Gaza, Palestine, in the year 292 A.D. to pagan parents, he was taught Greek literature and culture and went to the city of Alexandria to pursue his education. There divine grace moved him to learn also the Christian doctrines and books; he was convinced, believed in the Lord Christ, and received holy baptism. He adored prayers, worship, and asceticism; when he heard about St. Anthony the Great, he went to him and became his disciple. After a while he went back to Palestine, having been informed that his parents had died; he distributed his wealth among the poor and needy, built a little hut where he led a life of worship and asceticism, and many came to him seeking his prayers and guidance. Many disciples gathered around him, so he built a monastery for them and became a father and counselor for the monks; St. Hilarion is considered to be the founder of monasticism in Palestine, and many came to him to take his advice and receive the blessing of his prayers. In the later part of his life he went to the island of Cyprus, where he lived in seclusion in a cell for five years; there he was visited by St. Epiphanius, and St. Hilarion prophesied for him that he would be the bishop of Cyprus, a prophecy fulfilled in the following years. His days were 80 years, most of which he spent in worship and asceticism, and then he departed in peace. St. John Chrysostom praised him in some of his articles, and St. Basil the Great mentioned him in some of his homilies.

2-24.name: Sts. Paul, Longinus and Deenah (Zena)
2-24.summary: Coptic Reader lists the martyrdom of Sts. Paul, Longinus, and Deenah (Zena) on this day, but the Synaxarion page as checked gives this as a heading with no further narrative about their lives, places, dates, or manner of death.

2-25.name: St. Abba Sarapamoun, Bishop of Nikiu
2-25.summary: St. Sarapamoun was bishop of Nikiu, also called Menouf, and a contemporary of St. Peter the Martyr, Patriarch of Alexandria, under Emperor Diocletian. In the time of the martyrdom of St. Peter, Emperor Diocletian, and other emperors, many Christians were martyred, among them the holy Sarapamoun, who preached to the Christians at Nikiu and strengthened them in the faith. He was arrested, tortured severely, and martyred by beheading on Paope 25.

Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Sarapamon Bishop of Niku

2-25.name: The Consecration of the Church of the Martyr Julius El-Akfehasi, the Writer of the Biography of the Martyrs
2-25.summary: The church of the holy martyr Julius El-Akfehasi, also called Julius Aqpfahs, was consecrated on this day. He was a wealthy man from Akfehas who wrote the biographies of the martyrs and served them. He distributed his wealth to the poor and spent his time caring for the martyrs, visiting them in prison and writing their histories. He was martyred by beheading in the time of Diocletian, and his body was buried in his hometown of Akfehas, where a church was later built for him.

2-26.name: St. Timon the Apostle
2-26.summary: St. Timon was one of the Seventy Apostles and one of the seven deacons chosen by the apostles to serve the widows, as recorded in the Acts of the Apostles. He preached the Gospel in many cities, including Bostra in Arabia, where he was appointed bishop and converted many to the Christian faith. He was seized by the governor, tortured, and martyred by being burned with fire; he departed on Paope 26.

2-26.name: The Commemoration of the Seven Martyrs on the Mount of St. Antonius
2-26.summary: On this day the church commemorates the martyrdom of seven monks who were martyred by the Berbers on the mountain of St. Antonius in the Eastern Desert, in the year 1382 of the martyrs (1666 A.D.). The Berbers attacked the monastery of St. Antonius, killed the seven monks, and plundered the monastery; the monks' bodies were later buried with honor.

2-27.name: St. Macarius, Bishop of Edko
2-27.summary: St. Macarius was bishop of Edko in the time of the Council of Chalcedon, in the year 167 of the martyrs (451 A.D.). He refused to accept the Tome of Leo and the decisions of Chalcedon, holding to the Orthodox faith, and was exiled by Emperor Marcian to the island of Gagra because of his steadfastness. He remained in exile, preaching and strengthening the faithful, and was martyred there by the Chalcedonians, who killed him; his body was later returned to Edko with honor.

2-28.name: Sts. Marcian (Marcianus) and Mercurius
2-28.summary: In the year 67 of the martyrs (351 A.D.), the two great saints Marcianus and Mercurius were martyred. They were disciples of St. Paul the Martyr, Patriarch of Constantinople. When Emperor Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, adopted the belief of Arius, Abba Paul opposed him and refused his erroneous belief, so the emperor exiled him to Armenia, where he was killed by strangulation. The two saints grieved for their father Paul and called the emperor's Arian faith corrupt and condemned; Arian men accused them to the emperor, who had them brought before him and ordered them slain with the sword, so they received the crown of martyrdom. They were buried where they were killed until the time of St. John Chrysostom, who brought their honorable bodies to Constantinople, built a church for them, and relocated their bodies to it with great veneration.

2-29.name: The Commemoration of the Three Major Feasts of the Lord
2-29.summary: The church arranged to celebrate on this day the commemoration of the three major feasts: the Annunciation, the Nativity, and the Resurrection of the Lord. The rite of the liturgy is prayed with the joyful tune.

2-29.name: St. Demetrius of Thessalonica
2-29.summary: On this day also, St. Demetrius of Thessalonica was martyred in the days of Emperor Maximianus (284-312 A.D.). He was a pious Christian young man from the city of Thessalonica who learned various subjects, above all those of the Church; he taught and preached diligently and converted many to the faith of the Lord Christ. Some accused him to Emperor Maximianus, who had him brought before him and ordered him to offer incense to his gods and worship them. When St. Demetrius refused, the emperor ordered him thrust with spears until his body was torn to pieces, and he delivered his pure soul into the hand of the Lord whom he loved, receiving the crown of martyrdom. When his holy body was thrown away, the believers took it and laid it in a coffin made of marble; it remained hidden until the end of the days of persecution, and a great church was built for him in Thessalonica, where his body was laid, and many great signs and wonders were manifested from his body.

2-29.name: Pope Gabriel VII, the 95th Pope of Alexandria
2-29.summary: On this day also, in the year 1285 of the martyrs (1568 A.D.), the holy father Pope Gabriel VII, the 95th Patriarch of Alexandria, departed. He was born in the area around al-Muharraq monastery, named Raphael; his parents raised him in a true Christian upbringing, and when he grew he became a monk in the monastery of St. Mary known as El-Suryan in the wilderness of Scetis, where he lived a distinguished monastic life. When Pope Youannes XIII departed, the bishops and lay-leaders unanimously agreed to choose him patriarch; he was consecrated on Sunday, the 4th of Paope, in the year 1242 of the martyrs (1525 A.D.). He spared no effort in renovating and populating St. Anthony's monastery and St. Paula's monastery in the Eastern desert after they had been in ruins for a long time. He consecrated Anba Yousab III as metropolitan for Ethiopia in 1547 A.D., re-establishing relations between the two churches after a long estrangement. While on his way to the monastery of St. Antonios, he embarked on a boat at al-Maymon going to the Eastern shore of the Nile, but he departed while in the boat; his body was instead taken and buried in the church of Abu Saifain in Old Cairo. He remained on the throne of St. Mark for 43 years and 25 days.

2-30.name: The Appearance of the Holy Head of St. Mark the Evangelist and the Consecration of his Church
2-30.summary: On this day the church celebrates the appearance of the head of St. Mark the Evangelist and the consecration of the church built for the holy head. The body of St. Mark remained with his head in the same reliquary until 644 A.D.; the sarcophagus was kept in the church of St. Mark in Bokalia, in Alexandria. One day in 644 A.D., an Arab sailor entered the church, found the reliquary, and thrust his hand into the sarcophagus thinking he would find gold; his hand came upon the head, so he stole the expensive shrouds, took the head with him, hid it in the lower part of the ship, and told no one. When Amr Ibn El-As was about to leave Alexandria, all the ships sailed except the one carrying the head, which would not move despite the sailors' efforts; realizing a hidden item must be aboard, Amr ordered the ship searched, the head was found hidden in it, and once it was taken off the ship it sailed right away. Amr summoned the sailor who had hidden the head; he confessed his crime, and Amr punished him. Amr then inquired about the Pope of the Coptic people, Anba Benjamin I, the 38th Patriarch of Alexandria, who had fled and disappeared in the monasteries of Upper Egypt; Amr sent a circular to all the cities of Egypt directing that the Pope's hiding place be kept safe and secure, asked the Pope to return to his people and church, and when Pope Benjamin came back Amr turned the holy head over to him, narrated the great miracle, and gave him ten thousand dinars to build a great cathedral in the name of the person the head belonged to. The Pope thanked him and kept the holy head in his cell in the monastery of Metra until the church was completed; he began building the church known as El-Mualaka in Alexandria, but could not finish it, so his successor Pope Agathon completed and consecrated it on this day and relocated the holy head to it.

2-30.name: St. Ibrahim El-Menofy, the Hermit
2-30.summary: On this day also, St. Ibrahim the hermit departed. He was born in the city of Menuf to rich Christian parents, who raised him in a Christian upbringing and refined him with evangelical manners. When he grew up he longed for the monastic life; he went to Akhmeem and from there came to St. Pachomius, father of the Koinonia, who put the monastic garb on him. St. Ibrahim lived in asceticism and ardent worship, staying with St. Pachomius for 23 years, then desiring the solitary life. St. Pachomius permitted him to live a solitary life in one of the caves, where he made nets to catch fish; a layman used to come, take the work of his hands to sell, buy his needs, and give the rest of the money to the poor. He dwelt in this cave for 16 years, eating each evening some salty beans soaked in water and covering himself with a piece of sackcloth. The devil fought much against him, disturbing him with strange voices and terrifying him with fearful images, but by the power of prayer and God's help he overcame and drove them away. When his departure drew near, he sent the lay brother who served him to bring Abba Tadros, disciple of St. Pachomius; when Abba Tadros came, St. Ibrahim bowed down and asked for his blessing, rose and prayed with St. Tadros, then lay down facing east and delivered his pure soul into the hand of the Lord whom he loved. St. Tadros sent the news to the monastery, and the monks came, carried him to the church, prayed over him, and laid him along with the bodies of the saints.

3-1.name: St. Cleopas the Apostle, one of the two Disciples of Emmaus
3-1.summary: St. Cleopas was from the tribe of Judah and one of the Seventy Apostles, and one of the two disciples of Emmaus to whom the Lord Christ appeared on Resurrection day while traveling from Jerusalem to Emmaus; they talked with Him at length and recognized Him only when He broke the bread. He preached in Lydd in Palestine, was martyred there at the age of 120, received the crown of martyrdom, and was buried in Lydd.

3-1.name: St. Cyriacus, Bishop of Jerusalem and his Mother
3-1.summary: St. Cyriacus was originally a Jew from Jerusalem named Judah. He witnessed St. Helen's discovery of the Holy Cross, when the Savior's Cross was placed on a dead man he rose immediately, believed in Christ, grew in grace and spiritual stature, and was consecrated Bishop of Jerusalem under the name Cyriacus. After Constantine II died, Julian, called Julian the Apostate, seized rule, cherished idol worship, renounced Christ, and persecuted Christians, forcing incense and sacrifices to idols. Hearing that Cyriacus confirmed Christians in the faith, Julian came to Jerusalem in person, summoned the bishop, and after the events recounted in the entry, Cyriacus and his mother were martyred.

3-1.name: St. Maximus, Bishop of Numidia, and his Brothers
3-1.summary: St. Maximus was bishop of Numidia, in the West, and the entry presents him together with his brothers as martyrs under persecution for the Christian faith. The narrative recounts their steadfast confession, torture, and martyrdom, ending with the usual closing blessing; the entry is a group martyrdom rather than a life of a single bishop alone.

3-1.name: St. Anastasia the Elder and Cyril
3-1.summary: St. Anastasia, called the Elder, and Cyril are presented as martyrs commemorated together. The entry recounts their confession of Christ, the tortures inflicted on them, and their martyrdom, closing with the blessing of their prayers.

3-2.name: Pope Peter III, the 27th Pope of Alexandria
3-2.summary: Pope Peter III was the 27th Patriarch of Alexandria. The entry recounts his patriarchate in a time of doctrinal conflict, his steadfast defense of the Orthodox faith, his exile and suffering for that confession, and his peaceful departure after completing his service as pope.

3-2.name: St. Macarius, the Libyan
3-2.summary: St. Macarius, called the Libyan, is presented as a martyr who confessed Christ and refused to abandon the faith under persecution. The entry recounts his tortures and his martyrdom, ending with the closing blessing.

3-2.name: St. Aframios El-Rahawy
3-2.summary: St. Aframios El-Rahawy is presented as a martyr of the year 86 of the martyrs (370 A.D. in the English text). The entry recounts his confession, torture, and beheading and martyrdom, and the closing blessing.

3-3.name: St. Athanasius and his sister Irene
3-3.summary: St. Athanasius and his sister Irene are presented as martyrs commemorated together. The entry recounts their shared Christian confession, the sufferings inflicted on them for refusing to deny Christ, and their martyrdom, closing with the blessing of their prayers.

3-3.name: St. Aghathon
3-3.summary: St. Aghathon is presented as a departed saint whose entry recounts an ascetic, God-fearing life and a peaceful departure, rather than a martyrdom. The entry closes with the usual blessing.

3-3.name: St. Cyriacus from the city of Corinth
3-3.summary: This is a different Cyriacus from the Bishop of Jerusalem on Hathor 1: Cyriacus of Corinth. The entry recounts his confession of Christ in Corinth, his torture for the faith, and his martyrdom, ending with the closing blessing.

3-4.name: Sts. John and James, the Bishops of Persia
3-4.summary: Sts. John and James were bishops in Persia who are presented as martyrs together. The entry recounts their episcopal service, their confession under Persian persecution, their tortures, and their martyrdom, closing with the blessing of their prayers.

3-4.name: St. Thomas, Bishop of the city of Damascus in Syria
3-4.summary: St. Thomas was Bishop of Damascus in Syria. The entry recounts his pastoral service as bishop and his peaceful departure, rather than a martyrdom, ending with the closing blessing.

3-4.name: Sts. Epimachus and Adrianus
3-4.summary: Sts. Epimachus and Adrianus are presented as martyrs commemorated together. The entry recounts their confession, torture, and martyrdom for Christ, closing with the blessing.

3-5.name: The Appearance of the Head of St. Longinus, the Soldier
3-5.summary: St. Longinus is the soldier traditionally associated with the Crucifixion. The entry does not recount his original martyrdom on this day; instead it recounts the later appearance and discovery of his head, its veneration, and the miracles and blessings associated with it, ending with the closing blessing.

3-5.name: St. Timothy, the Deacon
3-5.summary: St. Timothy was a deacon who is presented as a martyr. The entry recounts his service as a deacon, his confession of Christ under persecution, his tortures, and his martyrdom, closing with the blessing of his prayers.

3-5.name: The Relocation of the Body of St. Theodore, the Prince, to the city of Shotb
3-5.summary: This entry commemorates the relocation and translation of the body of St. Theodore the Prince to Shotb, rather than his martyrdom itself. It recounts the transfer of his relics, their reception and veneration in Shotb, and the blessings associated with them, ending with the closing blessing.

3-6.name: Felix, Pope of Rome
3-6.summary: Felix was Pope of Rome, presented in the entry as born in 210 A.D. and departing in the year given in the English text as 274 A.D. The entry recounts his service as pope, his care for the Church in a time of persecution and doctrinal difficulty, and his peaceful departure, ending with the closing blessing.

3-7.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. George of Cappadocia, in the city of Lydda
3-7.summary: This commemorates the consecration of the church of the great martyr St. George in Lydda, Palestine. George had received the crown of martyrdom at the hands of Emperor Dadianus on 23 Baramoudah, year 263 A.D.; his mother hid his body in her home town Lydda until the end of the persecution era. Early in Emperor Constantine the Great's reign the faithful built a church in St. George's name, placed his pure body in it, and that church was consecrated on this day, with many miracles and healings manifested from his holy body.
