3-7.name: St. George, the Alexandrian
3-7.summary: This George of Alexandria was the nephew of Armanius, Governor of Alexandria. His father was a childless merchant in Alexandria who traveled to Lydda, attended the feast of the consecration of St. George the Martyr's church, prayed through that saint's intercession for a son, and was given a son whom he named George and raised with Christian education. After his parents died, his uncle the governor kept him until age 25; George guided his uncle's only daughter to the Christian faith after she heard monks praising and singing hymns near a monastery outside the city, explaining judgment, eternal punishment, and the righteous' felicity. Her father tried reasoning, promises, and threats, then ordered her beheaded, so she received martyrdom. When the governor learned George had convinced her, he tortured George severely, sent him to Ansena where its governor also tortured and finally beheaded him; Samuel the deacon took his body to Manf in El-Giza province, and his uncle's wife later placed it with her martyred daughter's body in Alexandria.

3-7.name: St. Nehroua (Naharua), of Fayyum
3-7.summary: St. Naharua was born in El-Fayyum in the later part of the third century, was Christian and feared God, and was martyred during Emperor Diocletian's reign. Hearing accounts of the martyrs, he went to Alexandria to die for the Lord Christ's name, was told in a vision to go to Antioch, and while wondering how to go, God's angel carried him from Alexandria to Antioch and set him before Diocletian, to whom he confessed Christ. Diocletian asked his name and country, marveled at how he had come, promised then threatened him without frightening him, and ordered torture by casting him to the lions and then burning his arms and feet with fire; finally his holy head was cut off, so he received the crown of martyrdom. St. Julius El-Akfehasi was present, took his body, shrouded it with great veneration, wrote his biography, and sent it with two of his men to his home town El-Fayyum.

3-7.name: Sts. Akebsyma, Itala and Joseph
3-7.summary: In year 92 of the martyrs (376 A.D.), Akebsyma, Itala, and Joseph were martyred. Akebsyma was bishop of Oneety in Persia, together with Joseph and Itala the deacon, and they faced persecution incited by Sapor, king of Persia. Seized and brought to Arbilla, they stood before the governor, who tried to persuade them to abandon the faith and threatened death if they would not worship the Sun; refusing, they were tortured, their bodies torn, and imprisoned, and they departed in prison and received the crown of martyrdom.

3-7.name: St. Mina, Bishop of Tamai (Thmoui) El-Amidid
3-7.summary: St. Mina was born in the later part of the seventh century in Samannoud, the only son of God-fearing parents who practiced fasting, prayers, and asceticism until their report was heard throughout the country. Grown up, he was made to marry against his will, but agreed with his wife to live in celibacy, practicing many worships for a while; later he agreed with her that she would live in a house of virgins. He went to the monastery of Anba Antonius in the Eastern desert, met Anba Mikhail before his ordination as a monk, and both went to the monastery of St. Macarius, becoming monks in the time of Anba Abraham and Anba Gawargah; Mina became their disciple and advanced in worship until he surpassed many. The Lord granted him healing the sick, his repute became well known, he was sorrowfully called to the episcopate, taught his people continually, and when he finished his good endeavor, departed in peace.

3-8.name: The Commemoration of the Four Incorporeal Creatures
3-8.summary: The Church arranged a celebration on this day to commemorate the four Incorporeal Creatures who carry the throne of God, as mentioned in the Book of Revelation. Ezekiel described them: a whirlwind from the North, the likeness of four living creatures, with faces of a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle; St. John the Evangelist said the four living creatures fell down and worshipped God on the throne, saying Amen, Alleluia. The Lord set them near His throne to make supplications for all creation, the man's face for the human race, the lion's for beasts, the ox's for cattle, and the eagle's for birds, and they are closer to God than all the heavenly orders; many Church teachers testified to their honor and built churches in their names.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Four Incorporeal Creatures
Watos Psali for the Four Incorporeal Creatures
Doxology for the Four Incorporeal Creatures
Fraction to the Father for the Feasts of the Virgin and Angels

3-8.name: St. Nikandros, Priest of Myra
3-8.summary: St. Nikandros was one of the apostolic fathers who enlightened the Church with their teachings in the first and second centuries. St. Titus, disciple of St. Paul the Apostle, ordained him priest for the city of Myra; he performed his duties well and brought many pagans back to the faith. When Governor Lybanius learned of him, he seized him and ordered idol worship, which Nikandros refused; cast into fire that did not harm him, he was finally ordered to have thick nails driven into his body and to be buried in a tomb, and after the soldiers did so he completed his strife and received the crown of life.

3-8.name: Father Pierius, Dean of the Theological School of Alexandria
3-8.summary: Father Pierius was head, or dean, of the Theological School of Alexandria during the papacy of Pope Theonas, the 16th Patriarch of Alexandria. He was a well-educated priest and eminent exegete and preacher of God's word, whom St. Jerome called Origen Junior. Renowned for voluntary poverty together with rich theological and philosophical knowledge, profound in spiritual contemplations, he wrote many treatises and sermons on various subjects, endured many hardships and tortures for faith in the Lord Christ, and spent the rest of his life in Rome, where he departed in peace.

3-9.name: The Assembly of the First Ecumenical Council at Nicea
3-9.summary: In year 41 of the martyrs (325 A.D.), the 318 fathers assembled at Nicea in Asia Minor during Emperor Constantine the Great's reign to judge Arius, a priest from Alexandria who taught that the Son of God was not equal in essence to God the Father and that there was a time when the Son did not exist. Pope Alexandros, 19th Pope of Alexandria, attended with his disciple, the learned deacon Athanasius. Constantine placed his royal scepter, sword, and seal before them, giving them authority to loose, bind, exile, or excommunicate. The fathers counted 319 present but only 318 visible chairs. Arius would not change his opinion, so they excommunicated him and all who shared his belief, put down the Nicene Creed, forbade adding to or taking away from it, commanded all believers to recite it in the Holy Liturgy and all prayers, and also put down other regulatory canons, then departed in peace.

3-9.name: Pope Isaac, the 41st Pope of Alexandria
3-9.summary: Pope Isaac's parents taught him church subjects and raised him with a Christian upbringing. As he grew, he read the biographies of saints and his heart inclined to monastic life. He went to the monastery of St. Macarius and became a disciple of the holy old monk Zacharias, who saw a cross of light over Isaac's head when he saw him, and received him with joy. Pope John III, the 40th Pope, asked for a monk to be his scribe and private secretary; those present recommended Father Isaac, and the Pope was well pleased with his knowledge and zeal. As Pope John III's departure drew near, he asked the Lord Christ to reveal his successor; the Lord told him in a vision that his disciple Isaac would sit on the throne after him, and the Pope told the people of the divine revelation. Pope John III departed in 689 A.D., and Isaac was enthroned on the 8th of Tobe, year 406 of the martyrs (690 A.D.). He enlightened the church with his teachings, restored many churches, especially the church of St. Mark the Evangelist in Alexandria and the patriarchal place attached to it, suffered many tribulations during his papacy, sat on the throne for three years, and then departed in peace.

3-9.name: The Consecration of the Great Cathedral in Abbasia - Cairo
3-9.summary: On this day in year 1735 of the martyrs, corresponding to November 18, 2018 A.D., the Cathedral of the great St. Mark the Apostle in the monastery of Anba Roweis in the Abbasia district of Cairo, the cathedral of the papal headquarters of the Egyptian Coptic Orthodox Church in the current era, was consecrated by Pope Tawadros II, 118th Pope, and about a hundred bishops and metropolitans of the Holy Synod. The story begins in the village of Al-Mawisat in Aswan Governorate, where extremists demolished the village's church on January 4, 1965 A.D. Its people complained to Pope Kyrillos VI, who called for the Holy Synod to convene; the council decided to refer the matter to President Gamal Abdel Nasser and assigned Bishop Samuel, Bishop of Services, to the task. When the president learned the truth, he asked how they would satisfy the Copts, and Bishop Samuel suggested a national decree to build a large new cathedral in the land of Anba Roweis, with the president himself laying the foundation stone. The president issued the decree and donated 100,000 Egyptian pounds toward construction costs. On July 24, 1965 A.D., the foundation stone was laid in the presence of President Nasser and Pope Kyrillos VI. On the occasion of nineteen centuries after the martyrdom of St. Mark, the cathedral was inaugurated on June 25, 1968 A.D., when the first Divine Liturgy was held in it. Pope Shenouda III added additions, such as two churches below it and central air conditioning. Pope Tawadros II decided to upgrade the cathedral to the highest level befitting the ancient Coptic Church; work continued for three years on upgrades, drawing icons according to Coptic heritage, creating a new iconostasis, and installing marble floors, lights, and audiovisual systems, until it was consecrated and Liturgy was prayed on this day.

3-10.name: The Fifty Virgins and Their Mother St. Sophia
3-10.summary: In the year 79 of the martyrs, in the days of the infidel Julian (363 A.D.), fifty virgins and their mother St. Sophia were martyred. They were in a convent near the city of El-Raha (Edessa), which was built by the mother of Emperor Constantine. They were pure, modest, humble, pious, and wise, and they were fasting and praying diligently. When the infidel Emperor Julian waged war against Shapur, king of Persia, he and his soldiers passed by the city of El-Raha; when his soldiers learned of the convent, they plundered it and killed all the virgins and their mother. Emperor Julian was also killed there, stabbed by a spear that they said was St. Mercurius's, and thus they received the crown of martyrdom.

3-10.name: The Assembly of a Council in Rome Because of the Glorious Feast of Theophany and the Great Lent
3-10.summary: A council assembled in Rome because of the glorious Feast of Theophany and the Great Lent. The bishop of Rome, St. Victor, agreed with the bishops who had gathered and wrote a letter to the bishops of the East, Asia, and Africa, calling for the celebration of the Feast of Theophany and the Great Lent together, as they are celebrated in Rome. The letter was delivered by a delegation led by St. Demetrius, the vine-dresser, 12th Pope of Alexandria, and they returned with the agreement of the bishops of the East, Asia, and Africa on the celebration of the Feast of Theophany and the Great Lent, as they are celebrated in Rome. The council also decided that the Feast of Theophany and the Great Lent should be celebrated on the same day in all churches, and that the bishops should not differ in their celebration. The letter was read in all churches, and the bishops agreed to the decision.

3-11.name: St. Anna (Hannah), the Mother of the Virgin
3-11.summary: St. Anna was from Bethlehem, of the tribe of Judah, and her father was Matthan, son of Melchi, of the tribe of Levi. Her mother was Mary, of the tribe of Judah, who had three daughters, one of whom was Hannah. Hannah married Joachim, and they prayed to God to grant them a child, like Hannah the mother of Samuel. God heard their prayer and granted them the Virgin Mary, the mother of God. Hannah was a kinswoman of Elizabeth, the mother of John the Baptist. She departed in peace.

3-11.name: St. Michael, the Monk
3-11.summary: St. Michael was from Domiat (Damietta), and he became a monk in the monastery of Anba Yehness in the wilderness of Scetis. The devil deceived him, and he went to Cairo, denied the faith, and married a non-Christian woman, remaining with her for eight days. He regretted his denial, went to a priest, confessed his sin, and was given a rule of repentance. He then went to the governor, confessed the Lord Christ, and was tortured severely. He was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

3-11.name: Sts. Archelaus and Elisha, the Hegumen
3-11.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the heading and a single line for this entry, with no further narrative: it states that the church celebrates the martyrdom of St. Archelaus and Abba Elisha, the Hegumen, followed by the closing blessing. No life, place, dates, or manner of death are given for them on this page.

3-12.name: The Honorable Archangel Michael
3-12.summary: This is the commemoration of the honorable Archangel Michael, head of the heavenly hosts. In the days of Pope Alexandros, 19th Pope, the people of Alexandria, unaware, celebrated a feast on 12th Hathor every year in a great temple of the star Zuhal (Saturn), offering sacrifices and distributing the meat to the poor. The patriarch gathered the Christians, explained that this was a pagan idol, and proposed demolishing the temple and replacing it with a feast of Michael, who intercedes for the waters, seeds, herbs, and air, with the custom of sacrifices continued as charity to the poor and needy in Michael's name. They agreed, demolished the temple, built a church, and consecrated it on 12th Hathor in the name of Michael, who was with the saints strengthening and comforting them until they completed their spiritual strife. As an example of his miracles, Dorotheus and his wife Theopista held the festival on the 12th of every month, but fell into hard times and took their clothes to sell. Michael appeared as an honorable man and commanded them not to sell them, but to go to a sheep-master and take a sheep worth one-third of a dinar, to a fisherman and take a fish worth one-third of a dinar but not slit its belly until he returned, and to a flour merchant and take flour as needed. When he returned, he slit the fish's belly and found in it a precious pearl, which they sold and paid their debts, and they continued to hold the festival.
hymnIds: Doxology for Archangels Michael and Gabriel
Fraction to the Father for Archangel Michael
Archangel Michael (12th of Every Coptic Month)

3-12.name: St. John (Youhanna), the Syrian
3-12.summary: St. John was one of the eminent Syrian monks, who departed in year 254 of the martyrs (538 A.D.). He was born just after his father's death, and his pious mother raised him. He became a monk in the monastery of Mar Thomas the Apostle in Seleucia, Syria, grew in monastic life, and excelled in church subjects. He established another monastery on the bank of the Euphrates in 530 A.D., went to Constantinople, studied Greek literature, wrote several books, commentaries on the Holy Scriptures, on the Virginal Birth, on the glorious Resurrection, and some homilies about the martyrs, and departed in peace.

3-13.name: The Honorable Archangel Gabriel
3-13.summary: The church celebrates the commemoration of Archangel Gabriel, the Announcer. He announced to Zacharias the priest the birth of St. John the Baptist, and announced to the Virgin Lady St. Mary the birth of the Savior of the World. Therefore the church gave him the title, the angel of Annunciation, the Herald of Glad Tidings.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for Archangel Gabriel the Announcer
Watos Psali for Archangel Gabriel the Announcer
Doxology for Archangels Michael and Gabriel

3-13.name: Pope Zacharias, 64th Pope of Alexandria
3-13.summary: In year 748 of the martyrs (1032 A.D.), the saintly Pope Zacharias, 64th Patriarch of Alexandria, departed. He was born in Alexandria, disciplined with Christian morals, and because of his piety they ordained him a priest; he followed a good conduct in his life, so everyone loved him. When Pope Phillotheous, 63rd Pope, departed, the bishops and lay-leaders assembled and unanimously agreed to elect him patriarch; he was consecrated on 20th Tobe, year 720 of the martyrs (1004 A.D.). Abba Zacharias suffered many tribulations: El-Hakem imprisoned him for three months, then cast him to the lions, which did not harm him, as with Daniel the prophet. He threatened him often with death. Finally, because of the mediation of one of the princes, he released him. Abba Zacharias went to the desert of Scete, to the monastery of St. Macarius, where he stayed for nine years. During these years the Christians suffered many hardships: they slew many of them, plundered their homes, and demolished several churches, including the church of St. Mercurius in Ma-asaret Helwan and the monastery of Barsome the Naked. El-Khalifa visited this monastery often, for he had a cordial relation with the monks; the monks took the chance of his presence and solicited a pardon for the return of Pope Zacharias. Abba Zacharias lived 12 years after his return from the desert, during which he renovated churches, restored those that were destroyed, and served his people. He remained in the papacy for 28 years and departed to the Lord in peace.

3-13.name: St. Tadros Tyro
3-13.summary: Also on this day, in year 22 of the martyrs (306 A.D.), St. Tadros Tyro departed; Tyro is the surname of his family. He was a soldier in the Roman army, and he refused to have fellowship with his fellow soldiers in practicing pagan worship. The commander of his unit summoned him and asked him the reason for his refusal; St. Tadros declared that he was Christian. When he threatened to slay him, he affirmed his commitment, saying that the Lord Jesus Christ is his God and that even if his body were dismembered, God would accept it as a sacrifice. The commander sent him away for a short while that he might change his conviction; he summoned him again, offering many incitements, but he did not renounce his faith. He suffered many tortures that he thankfully endured, for it is the fellowship of sufferings with the passion of the Lord Christ. When they imprisoned him, God sent His angel to comfort him. They summoned him for a third time and burned him alive, so he received the crown of martyrdom. One of the believing women buried his body.

3-13.name: St. Timothy, Bishop of Ansena (Antinoe)
3-13.summary: On this day also, the saint Abba Timothy, Bishop of Ansena (Antinoe or Antinopolis), departed. This father was born in the later part of the third century, in a Christian family, and he was raised in the fear of God. He became a monk, grew in virtues, and was ordained bishop of Ansena. He shepherded his flock well, taught them the Orthodox faith, and persevered in fasting, prayer, and worship. He departed in peace.

3-13.name: Anba Yousab (Joseph), in El-Assas Mountain
3-13.summary: Anba Yousab was a native of Faw, an only child, brought up in a Christian manner. He often visited the monastery of Anba Pachomius, Father of Koinonia, and grace moved him to join the monastery and become a monk. He grew in piety and asceticism, and was given the gift of healing the sick, so many came to him. Fearing he would lose his labor, he prayed that God would guide him to a path, and afterwards he went to El-Assas Mountain, lived a solitary life in a cave, completed his good endeavor, and departed in peace. God revealed many signs and wonders from his pure body.

3-14.name: St. Martinus, Bishop of Tours
3-14.summary: St. Martinus was from Greece, an ascetic worshipper, who resisted the followers of Arius for a long time, who wanted to slay him. He lived in a cave near the shore of the Mediterranean Sea, his virtues spread, and he was chosen bishop of Tours. He lived an apostolic life, and God honored him with many signs. As a miracle, during a funeral procession, a man stopped it, claiming the deceased owed him a big sum; Martinus entreated him to let the procession go, but the man refused. Martinus prayed to God to make the truth known, the dead man rose and rebuked the falsely accusing man, exposing his lies; the unjust man died, the raised man went home and lived many years, and Martinus finished his good endeavor and departed in peace.

3-14.name: The Officer Faros and the Six Hermits
3-14.summary: Officer Faros and six ascetic fathers from Mount Thebes were martyred. Faros was a senior officer in the army of Emperor Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century, when persecution escalated against Christians everywhere, especially in Egypt. The Colesian governor violently attacked and persecuted Christians, sent soldiers who seized six ascetic hermits from Mount Thebes and imprisoned them. Faros went at night, untied and released them, asking them to pray that he might share in their martyrdom, for he was a senior officer but feared to confess the Lord Christ because of the severity of tortures. Soldiers recaptured the six and brought them before the governor, who tried to force them to raise incense to idols; they refused. Suddenly Faros rushed in, confessed the Lord Christ, and defended the hermits. The governor befriended him, and when he failed, ordered him tortured severely until his body was torn, and he received the crown of martyrdom. The six hermits, after being tortured extensively, were ordered beheaded by the governor and received the crown. He ordered their bodies thrown outside the city to be devoured by beasts, but the beasts did not come near them; believers came, carried the bodies to the church, prayed, and buried them with great veneration.

3-15.name: St. Mari-Mina, the Wonder-Worker
3-15.summary: St. Mina was martyred in year 25 of the martyrs (309 A.D.). He was born in Nikiu about the middle of the third century; his father Eudoxius was governor of the city of Nikiu, and his mother was Euphemia. His brother Anatolius, envious, brought accusations against his father before the Emperor, who transferred him to govern the area of North Africa, the District of Marriot, where the people were pleased with him as merciful and God-fearing. His mother Euphemia was pious, prayed and fasted diligently, and, being barren, entreated the Lord Christ to grant her a godly offspring, fasting till evening and offering large alms to the poor and needy. On the feast of the Dormition of the Holy Virgin, she went to the church of the Virgin at Atribes, saw multitudes entering with joy, sighed and wept before the icon of Our Lady St. Mary, entreating her intercession to grant her a son, and heard a voice coming out of the icon saying Amen. She rejoiced, returned home after the Divine Liturgy, told her godly husband Eudoxius, and shortly afterwards Euphemia conceived. At his birth she wanted to call him Blodianus after his grandfather, but his mother refused because of the word Amen heard from the icon of the Holy Virgin, and called him Mina, saying Mina has the same letters as Amen. His parents reared him in a spiritual manner, instructed him in church teachings, and he read the Bible and frequently went to church, growing in piety and moral excellence. At age 11 his father departed in 296 A.D., and his mother departed three years later; he inherited a great fortune and distributed much of it to the poor and needy. About 300 A.D. he enlisted in the army, and the commander, a friend of his father, made him second in command; everyone loved him for his gentleness and piety. When Emperors Diocletian and Maximianus issued an edict to worship idols and persecute Christians, Mina left his position, distributed the rest of his wealth to the poor and needy, went to the desert to enjoy divine communion with God in pure worship, and stayed in the wilderness about five years, worshipping with many fasts and prayers day and night. One night a voice told him to go to the city and confess the Lord Christ before the governor, foretelling three crowns: virginity, worship and asceticism, and martyrdom. He left the wilderness, returned to the city, and publicly confessed the Name of the Lord Christ before the governor in the midst of a great multitude. The governor ordered him apprehended and imprisoned; the next day he was brought and tried to be appeased, since he was of noble kinship, to worship idols, with promises of honors and precious gifts. When the governor failed to persuade him, he tortured him in many different ways, then imprisoning him. The Lord Christ appeared, comforted and encouraged him, and healed his wounds. The governor, weary of torturing him, wrote a decree ordering him beheaded and his pure body burned in fire. Soldiers took him to the place of execution; he raised his eyes to heaven, prayed fervently, extended his neck, and the swordsman beheaded him, and he received the crown of martyrdom. They tried to burn his pure body, but it stayed in the fire three days and three nights and was not harmed; believers came, took his body from the middle of the fire, shrouded it in expensive shrouds, and buried it with great veneration.

3-15.name: St. John, El-Rabban (Priest-Monk)
3-15.summary: St. John was a disciple of Anba Hadid the priest, born in Cairo to godly parents who were merciful to sojourners and the poor. He grew longing for monastic life, frequently visited el-Shahran monastery, and became a disciple of the holy monk El-Rabban Ibrahim. Later he went to Jerusalem and dwelt in the monastery of John the Baptist for three years, persevering in worship and spiritual fight, then returned again to the monastery of El-Shahran. His spiritual father advised him to go to Anba Hadid the presbyter, and he went to him in the city of Matobus El-Roman and dwelt with him, gathering Christian children in the church and teaching them reading, writing, and the Holy Scripture, striving in fasting, prayer, and long vigils. Anba Hadid saw his disciple John grown in grace and nominated him for the priesthood; he received the priestly rank and served the congregation faithfully. God granted him the gift of healing the sick, and he healed many. Satan, envious, brought him many tribulations, which he endured patiently. Finally he settled in the city of Samanoud, finished his good endeavor, departed in peace, and the faithful buried him in the church of Samanoud.

3-16.name: The Beginning of the Fast of the Nativity (Advent)
3-16.summary: Today marks the beginning of the fast of the Nativity, the Advent, in the Coptic Orthodox Church, which is concluded by the feast of the Nativity of the Good Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ. The entry implores the Lord, who fulfilled salvation by emptying Himself according to the economy to redeem the human race, to help the faithful do what is pleasing to Him during this holy fast and through all the days of their lives, and to accept their fasts and prayers.

3-16.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Abu-Nofer (Onuphrius) the Hermit
3-16.summary: This entry concerns the church of St. Abu-Nofer (Onuphrius) the Hermit in El-Zaher, Cairo. Abu-Nofer lived in the inner wilderness for 60 years and did not see the face of a human, reaching a high spiritual rank as an anchorite, living in the wilderness beside a palm tree and a spring of water; the palm yielded twelve clusters of dates a year, one of which was enough food for a month. Near the end of his life, St. Paphnoutius the Ascetic visited him and wrote his biography for the spiritual benefit of all generations. When Abu-Nofer departed, Paphnoute shrouded and buried him in his cave, and churches were built after the name of St. Abu-Nofer.
hymnIds: The Great Saint Abba Nopher (Hathor 16, Paone 16)

3-16.name: St. Yostus, the Bishop
3-16.summary: Coptic Reader gives only a short narrative for this entry, with no further life details: it states that St. Yostus, the bishop, was martyred by the hands of Maximus the prince, who tortured him severely for the sake of the faith, and finally he received the crown of martyrdom, followed by the closing blessing. No birthplace, dates, or other life events are given on this page.

3-16.name: Pope Mina II, the 61st Patriarch of the SEE of St. Mark
3-16.summary: On this day also, in year 691 of the martyrs (974 A.D.), the Holy Father Pope Mina II, 61st Patriarch of the See of St. Mark, departed. He was born and raised in a village called Sandala to Christian parents. When he grew, they forced him to get married against his will; nevertheless, he agreed with his wife to live a celibate life. Then he took her permission and went to the wilderness of Shiheet, where he became a monk in the monastery of St. Macarius and lived a virtuous life. After the departure of Pope Theophanes, 60th Patriarch, the bishops and people agreed on choosing Fr. Mina for the patriarchate; he was consecrated on 11th Koiahk, year 673 of the martyrs (956 A.D.). Some people opposed him under the pretense that he was married; however, when they realized that he did not know his wife as married people do, they changed their view, considered him worthy of his rank, and obeyed him. This saint faced many tribulations, which he endured with patience, fasting, and prayers, and departed in peace after being on the throne for about 18 years.

3-16.name: St. Nilus of Sinai
3-16.summary: St. Nilus of Sinai departed on this day. He was born about the middle of the fourth century to a wealthy Christian family, grew adorned with many spiritual virtues, and excelled in literature and science, which made Emperor Theodosius the Great advance him to the highest ranks in the Empire. He married and had a son and a daughter, but desired the monastic life; he renounced all pleasures of this world, made an agreement with his wife, left Constantinople, and went to the monastery of Mount Sinai along with his son Theodulos. There they lived a life of solitude and asceticism; his wife and daughter lived in one of the convents. St. Nilus persevered in struggling against the devils, vanquished them with the might of God, gained extensive experience in spiritual warfare, and wrote letters of comfort and encouragement to some monks, telling them not to be frightened from the warfare of the evil spirits. He also has many other monastic sayings. When the barbarians invaded the monastery about the year 430 A.D., they took his son Theodulos captive and sold him as a slave in Palestine. St. Nilus was grieved, left the wilderness searching for his son, at last found him and brought him back to the monastery. St. Nilus persevered in worship and asceticism till he became advanced in age, and departed in peace in a good old age.

3-17.name: St. John Chrysostom
3-17.summary: John Chrysostom, the Golden Mouth, was born in Antioch in 347 and raised by his mother after his father's death. He studied rhetoric, embraced an ascetic life, was ordained deacon and then priest in Antioch, and became famous for his preaching. He became Patriarch of Constantinople, where his reforms and preaching brought him into conflict with powerful opponents, including Empress Eudoxia. He was exiled, and he departed in exile, a peaceful departure after a life of preaching, asceticism, and suffering for the faith.

3-17.name: St. Paul of the Danfeek Mount
3-17.summary: St. Paul was a holy monk associated with the Danfeek Mount, presented in the page as a man of asceticism and worship in the wilderness. The entry is comparatively short and focuses on his monastic life and good strife rather than on a detailed biography. He departed in peace, and the entry closes with the usual blessing.

3-18.name: St. Philip the Apostle
3-18.summary: Philip was one of the twelve apostles, from Bethsaida, and the page follows his preaching in Phrygia and Hierapolis, where he preached Christ and performed signs. He was opposed by idol-worshippers, was arrested, and, according to the page, was crucified upside down, though the narrative also says he was stoned and then crucified. He departed as a martyr-apostle, and the entry closes with the blessing.

3-18.name: The Two Saints: Atrasis and Yona (Junia)
3-18.summary: Atrasis and Yona, also given as Junia, were martyred for refusing to renounce Christ and worship idols. They were subjected to tortures, remained steadfast, and were finally beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom. The page presents them together as a single joint martyrdom entry, with no separate birthplace or life history given for either saint beyond their steadfast confession.

3-18.name: The Miracle of Moving the Mokattam Mountain
3-18.summary: This is a commemoration, not a saint's death. In the reign of the Fatimid Caliph Al-Muizz, after a challenge based on the Gospel words about faith moving mountains, the Church, led by Pope Abraham and the shoemaker Simon the Tanner, prayed and fasted for three days. Simon, identified in the page as a one-eyed tanner, instructed the people to cry Lord have mercy and to make the sign of the cross, and the Mokattam Mountain moved. The Caliph was amazed, and the Church commemorates the miracle and the faith of Simon and Pope Abraham.

3-19.name: The Consecration of the Church of Sts. Sergius and Bacchus
3-19.summary: This is a short consecration commemoration for the church of the two soldier-martyrs Sergius and Bacchus. The page gives no separate life or martyrdom narrative for Sergius and Bacchus on this day; it is presented as the consecration of their church, ending with the blessing.

3-19.name: St. Abibus
3-19.summary: Abibus was a deacon from Edessa who, with Guria and Shamouna mentioned in the entry, confessed Christ during persecution. He refused to sacrifice to idols, endured torture, and was burned, receiving the crown of martyrdom. The entry focuses on his steadfast confession and fiery martyrdom rather than on a long biography.

3-20.name: St. Anianus, the 2nd Pope of Alexandria
3-20.summary: Anianus was the shoemaker of Alexandria whose shoe St. Mark mended, and who, after hearing St. Mark preach, believed and was baptized with his household. St. Mark ordained him, and after St. Mark's martyrdom Anianus succeeded him as the second Patriarch of Alexandria. He shepherded the Church, ordained priests and deacons, and departed in peace after completing his service.

3-21.name: St. Gregory the Wonder Worker
3-21.summary: Gregory, Bishop of Neo-Caesarea in Pontus, was born to pagan parents, converted to Christianity, studied under Origen, and became bishop of his native city, where almost all the inhabitants were still pagan. By his teaching, holiness, and miracles, hence Wonder Worker, he converted the city, built churches, and organized its Christian life. He departed in peace, leaving a largely Christian city.

3-21.name: St. Cosma II, the 54th Pope of Alexandria
3-21.summary: Cosma II, also spelled Cosmas, was a monk before his election as the 54th Patriarch of Alexandria. The page presents him as a righteous, ascetic patriarch who shepherded the Church in humility and care for its people. He departed in peace after completing his patriarchate, and the entry closes with the blessing.

3-21.name: St. John El-Tabayse in the Assiut Mount
3-21.summary: John, also called John El-Assiouty, was born in Assiut in the early fifth century and became a monk in Scetis, where he lived under St. Isidore for five years. An angel then guided him to the Assiut Mountain, where he lived the rest of his life as a solitary in a cave, in asceticism and prayer. He departed in peace on the Assiut Mount.

3-21.name: The Holy Martyrs: Alphaeus, Zacchaeus, Romanus and John
3-21.summary: Coptic Reader gives only this heading and the statement that the Church also celebrates on this day the saints Thomas, Victor, and Isaac of the city of Ashmunein. No further narrative, place of martyrdom, or manner of death is given for either group on this page.

3-21.name: The Translocation of the Body of St. Yehnes (John) Kama, From His Monastery to the Syrian Monastery
3-21.summary: John Kama was a holy monk and founder associated with a monastery in the Wadi El-Natrun area, known for his ascetic life and for the monastery that bore his name. After his departure, his body was later transferred from his own monastery to the Syrian Monastery, and the Church commemorates that translocation on this day. The entry focuses on the transfer of his relics rather than on a full biography.

3-22.name: Sts. Cosmas, Demian, Their Brothers and Their Mother
3-22.summary: Cosmas and Demian were physician brothers, from Arabia in the page's account, who healed the sick without charge, relying more on prayer than on medicine. Under Diocletian, the prefect Lysias summoned them, learned they had three brothers, and summoned the brothers and their mother, ordering them to offer incense to idols. They refused, endured boiling water, a crushing wheel, chains and casting into the sea, from which an angel saved them, and later crucifixion, stoning, and arrows that turned back on the soldiers. Their mother was beheaded after encouraging them; the officer Victor, son of Romanus, buried her body and was himself exiled to Egypt and martyred there. Finally Lysias ordered Cosmas, Demian, and their brothers beheaded, and the faithful buried their bodies.

3-23.name: St. Cornelius the Centurion
3-23.summary: Cornelius was a Roman centurion of the Italian Regiment in Caesarea of Palestine who had formerly worshipped the stars. Hearing of the apostles' miracles, he forsook star-worship, prayed, fasted, and gave alms, praying for the Lord God to direct and guide him. At about the ninth hour an angel appeared to him, told him his prayers and alms had come up as a memorial before God, and sent him to Joppa for Simon Peter, lodging with Simon the tanner by the sea. Peter came to Caesarea, preached Christ's incarnation, redemption, crucifixion, resurrection, and ascension, and the Holy Spirit fell on Cornelius, his household, and those with him, who believed and were baptized. Cornelius then left military service, followed the apostles, was ordained by Peter as Bishop of Caesarea of Palestine, preached there, baptized many including Demetrius the governor, and after completing his good strife departed in peace.

3-23.name: The Consecration of the Church of the Martyr, St. Marina
3-23.summary: This is a short consecration commemoration for the church of the great martyr Marina, the chosen bride of Christ, in the city of Antioch. After the end of pagan worship and during the reign of the righteous Emperor Constantine, the church was built in the same place where her pure body was located. No life or martyrdom narrative for Marina herself is given on this page beyond that statement.

3-24.name: The Twenty-Four Presbyters
3-24.summary: The Church commemorates the twenty-four incorporeal priests of the Truth who sit around God's throne. St. John the Revealer saw them in Revelation: around the throne were twenty-four thrones, with twenty-four elders in white robes and gold crowns, who fall down, cast their crowns before the throne, and worship Him who lives forever. Each has a harp and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints, and they sing a new song, You are worthy to take the scroll, and to open its seals. The page describes them as luminous priests from the spiritual heavenly orders who intercede for humanity and offer the saints' prayers as incense before God, and notes that the fathers of the Church arranged this feast to commemorate them.

3-24.name: Bishop Narcees, and St. Thecla
3-24.summary: In the year 59 of the martyrs (343 A.D.), the Holy Father St. Narcees was martyred. He was bishop of Seleucia in Mesopotamia, on the west bank of the Tigris River, during the reign of Sapor II, king of Persia. Along with him St. Thecla and about twenty others were martyred. The page gives no further details about the manner of their martyrdom beyond that they were martyred.

3-24.name: St. Proclus, Patriarch of Constantinople
3-24.summary: Proclus was born in Constantinople around 390 A.D., brought up in piety, and, because of his knowledge and intellect, was loved by the people and ordained a priest; Father Sisinius I, Patriarch of Constantinople, consecrated him a bishop, and he served the people with humility and devotion. When Sisinius departed, Emperor Theodosius intervened to appoint Nestorius as his successor; Proclus attended the Ecumenical Council of Ephesus in 431 A.D., which excommunicated Nestorius, and Maximian was then appointed patriarch but departed in 434 A.D. The people unanimously chose Proclus as Patriarch of Constantinople, and he received congratulatory epistles from Pope Cyril I, Pillar of Faith, and the other patriarchs. He took up his pastoral duties after the disturbances caused by Nestorius's excommunication, dealt with the situation with wisdom, humility, and meekness, guarded the Orthodox faith, sent pastoral epistles, urged adherence to St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory of Nazianzus, and praised St. Cyril's epistles as a complete document of the faith of the universal church. He also relocated the relics of St. John Chrysostom from his exile in Comana to the Church of the Apostles in Constantinople, and during violent earthquakes in surrounding countries he went himself among the afflicted, sharing their pain and adding asceticism, fasting, and prayer. After finishing his good endeavor, he departed in peace in the year 163 of the martyrs (447 A.D.).

3-25.name: St. Mercurius, known as Abu Saifain
3-25.summary: St. Mercurius was from Rome, the son of pious parents Gordianus and Philopater; his father Philopater was a soldier and priest who died a martyr, after which Mercurius became a soldier and leader of the army and was called Abu Saifain, Father of Two Swords, because an angel gave him another sword in battle. When Emperor Decius denied God, Mercurius refused to worship the idols, was stripped of his rank and office, and was tortured with burning, iron nails, and a sword-like saw. The Lord strengthened him, and the next day he was brought before the Emperor, who offered him a choice between the priesthood of idols and torture; Mercurius refused the idols and was beheaded in Caesarea, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

3-26.name: Sts. Valerian and Tiburtius, his Brother
3-26.summary: On this day in the year 91 of the martyrs (375 A.D.), St. Valerian, St. Tiburtius his brother, and St. Maximus were martyred. Valerian was a Christian who preached the Lord Jesus Christ and was cast before the lions, which did not harm him, and Maximus was present and also martyred. Tiburtius, who was a Christian, was tortured and then beheaded with his brother Valerian, and Maximus was also martyred with them.

3-26.name: St. Gregory of Nyssa, brother of St. Basil the Great
3-26.summary: St. Gregory of Nyssa was the younger brother of St. Basil the Great; his father was a bishop, and his mother was Emmelia, a holy woman. Gregory was educated in the sciences and theology, was ordained a priest, and later became Bishop of Nyssa, where he shepherded his flock with wisdom and taught them the orthodox faith. He was present at the Council of Constantinople in 381 A.D., was exiled for a time by the Arians, and later returned to his see. He died in peace after a life of teaching and defending the faith, and his departure is commemorated on this day.

3-27.name: St. James, the Persian
3-27.summary: St. James the Persian was a noble Persian who served in the court of King Yazdegerd I and, under pressure, denied Christ and worshipped the sun and fire, but his mother and wife rebuked him and he repented and returned to the Christian faith. When the king learned of his return, he ordered James to be cut into pieces, joint by joint, beginning with his fingers and toes, and James endured the tortures with patience, praying and encouraging himself. He was finally beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom, and his body was taken and buried with honor.

3-27.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Victor, Ebn-Romanus
3-27.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of the church of St. Victor, son of Romanus (Ebn-Romanus), in the city of Asyut in Upper Egypt. St. Victor was a soldier and martyr who suffered for the Christian faith under Diocletian and was beheaded. The church built in his name was consecrated on this day, and the entry closes with the blessing of his prayers.

3-28.name: St. Sarapamon, Bishop of Niku
3-28.summary: St. Sarapamon was Bishop of Niku in Egypt during the reign of Diocletian, and he was known for his piety, ascetic life, and care for his flock. When the persecution began, he was arrested and brought before the governor, where he confessed Christ and refused to sacrifice to idols. He was tortured severely, including being hung and beaten, but remained steadfast in the faith. He was finally beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom, and his body was buried with honor by the faithful.

3-29.name: St. Peter, the Seal of the Martyrs, 17th Pope of Alexandria
3-29.summary: Pope Peter I, called the Seal of the Martyrs, was martyred in the year 28 of the martyrs (312 A.D.). His parents, like Zacharias and Elizabeth, were childless and righteous before God, and Peter was born after many fervent prayers; at age 7 he was handed to Pope Theonas, was educated in the theological school, was ordained deacon at 12 and priest at 16, and became dean of the Theological School of Alexandria. After Theonas' departure he was consecrated Pope Peter I, the 17th pope, on the first day of Mesor in the 18th year of the martyrs (302 A.D.); he toured Egypt confirming believers, brought back those who strayed, laid down church canons, and excommunicated Arius after repeatedly advising him to abandon his heretical teachings. Emperor Maximianus, co-ruler of Diocletian, came to Egypt, slew many people and destroyed churches and cities, then captured Peter, imprisoned him, and ordered him slain; the people gathered at the prison to save him by force, so the captain postponed the execution. Peter refused to absolve Arius, telling the priests that Christ had appeared to him in a vision wearing a torn robe and said Arius had rent His robe by separating Him from His Father. Peter secretly arranged with the captain to be taken out through a hole dug in the prison wall on the side where there were no people, was brought near the tomb of St. Mark the Evangelist, prayed that his blood would mark the end of paganism and of shedding Christians' blood, heard a heavenly voice say Amen, and was beheaded by the swordsman. Believers dressed his body in pontifical vestments, seated it on the throne of St. Mark, which he had refused to sit on in life, prayed the funeral rites, and buried him with great veneration.

3-29.name: St. Clement, Pope of Rome
3-29.summary: St. Clement I, bishop of Rome, was martyred in 100 A.D. He was born in Rome in the first half of the first century to an honorable father who was a member of the Roman Senate, was cultured in Greek literature, and excelled in various subjects. He became a disciple of the apostle St. Paul, was baptized, was recruited by Paul to assist him in service, was mentioned by Paul in his epistle to the Philippians, and was consecrated bishop for Rome about 93 A.D. during Emperor Domitian's reign, bringing many people to faith in Christ. Under Emperor Trajan, hearing that a noble Roman had become bishop and attracted many to Christianity, he exiled Clement to the Crimean Peninsula, to the city of Chersonesus, to work in a stone quarry, where Clement met thousands of banished Christians, became a compassionate father to them, and turned the place of exile into a center for worship and preaching. When the city governor learned this, he tied Clement's neck to an anchor and cast him into the sea so nothing would remain to comfort the faithful; in this way Clement delivered up his pure spirit and received the crown of martyrdom.

3-29.name: St. Catherine of Alexandria
3-29.summary: St. Catherine of Alexandria was martyred in the year 23 of the martyrs (307 A.D.). She was born to pagan Egyptian parents in Alexandria in the latter part of the third century, about 288 A.D., and was called Zorothia; God granted her dazzling beauty and superior intelligence, and she diligently studied Philosophy, Poetry, Music, Mathematics, Astronomy, and Medicine, through which she realized the falsehood and corruption of pagan worship, and divine grace moved her heart to seek the truth. In a night vision she saw the Virgin St. Mary carrying the Child Jesus, went to a Christian priest for guidance, was told that the Lord Christ wants her to be His daughter, studied the Holy Bible with that priest, and was baptized with the name Catherine, meaning Many Crowns. After baptism she longed to confirm believers in Christ; Emperor Maxentius, enraged at her account, sent men to bring her to the pagan temple where he was, she admonished him for his delusion and ignorance, and he was amazed at her courage and dazzled by her beauty. He arranged for fifty of the best pagan scholars to debate her, but by God's grace she won the debate, convinced them of the Christian faith, all accepted Christ as Savior, and the Emperor ordered them burned alive, receiving martyrdom crowns. He spared Catherine because he was preoccupied with her beauty and hoped she would become his wife, but she refused all his proposals and remained steadfast; he then had her scourged, severely tortured, and imprisoned, and asked his wife to persuade her. His wife went to prison with Prophyrius the commander, Catherine explained the Christian faith to them, they believed and received holy baptism. When the Emperor returned he ordered his wife and Prophyrius beheaded and Catherine tortured atrociously, yet the Lord comforted and filled her with peace; she was finally beheaded at about 19 years of age and received the crown of martyrdom. She was buried in Alexandria, then monks relocated her relics to Mount Sinai, where her body is in the present time in the monastery named after her in the wilderness of Sinai.

3-30.name: St. Macarius
3-30.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the heading and a single sentence for this entry, with no further narrative: it states that the church celebrates the commemoration of the martyrdom of St. Macarius, followed by the closing blessing. No life, place, date, or manner of death beyond that sentence is given on this page.

3-30.name: The Monk St. John El-Qalyuby
3-30.summary: St. John El-Qalyuby, the monk, was martyred in the year 1298 of the martyrs (1582 A.D.). He was a native of Qalyub and became a monk in the monastery of St. Pishoy in the wilderness of Shiheet; he went to Cairo to take care of some monastery needs, where Muslims seized him and wanted to force him to abandon his Christian faith, but he stood fast in his belief. They sentenced him to be ridden on a camel and paraded through the streets of Cairo, stabbed him with sharp knives in his hands and shoulders, and he endured all these tortures patiently. When they saw his steadfastness, they nailed him to a cross until he delivered his spirit into the Lord's hand and received the crown of martyrdom; believers took his body down from the cross, brought it to the church of St. Barbara in Old Cairo, shrouded him in expensive shrouds, prayed over him, and buried him in that church in the presence of a great multitude of Christians.

3-30.name: St. Acacius, Patriarch of Constantinople
3-30.summary: St. Acacius, Patriarch of Constantinople, departed on this day. He was knowledgeable and well informed about the Holy Books and their interpretation and was ordained a priest for the church of Constantinople; when the Council of Chalcedon convened and issued its decisions and decrees, he was not pleased and was disturbed by what befell St. Dioscorus. When Anatolius, Patriarch of Constantinople, departed, Acacius was chosen to succeed him, strove diligently to eliminate the division and enmity in the church, and, finding the spiritual ailment deep-rooted and because of his ill health, devoted his efforts to the salvation of his own soul. He sent an epistle to Anba Peter III, the 27th Pope of Alexandria, confessing the true faith he had learned and received from the Holy Fathers St. Cyril and St. Dioscorus, followed it with many others asking the Pope of Alexandria to accept him in fellowship, and Pope Peter replied with a letter sent with three bishops who went to Constantinople disguised, were received by Acacius with great joy, and all participated in the Divine Liturgy. When the three bishops returned to Egypt and handed Acacius' letter to Pope Peter, Peter accepted it with joy and ordered Patriarch Acacius to be mentioned in the Divine Liturgies. When the news reached the Chalcedonian bishops, they exiled Acacius from Constantinople, and he remained in exile steadfast in the Orthodox faith until he departed in peace.

3-30.name: The Consecration of the Church of Saints Cosmas, Demian, Their Brothers and Their Mother
3-30.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of the church of Saints Cosmas and Demian, their brothers Anthonius, Leontius, and Euprepius, and their mother Theodota. The church was built by Emperor Justinian in Constantinople as a splendid and magnificent church, as a thanksgiving offering and in recognition of the good deed these saints had done for him: he had been grievously ill and close to death, the two saints appeared to him and healed him from his sickness, so he built the church as a memorial and acknowledgment of their favor.
